10563-good-intentions-ship-s-company-par:
W. W. Jacobs published this comic tale as the third part of Ship's Company, narrated by a night-watchman with a broom lashed to a crane. Jealousy, he says, is the cause: his wife sets traps, asks others to watch him, and once claimed a girl he saved from a bus had not slipped at all. Jacobs writes in salty, first-person humor.

The watchman insists you cannot argue with jealous people or shame them, and his tales of marriage, traps, and eyes blacked in folly fill the piece. Good intentions lead to comic trouble at every turn. Readers get a short, witty Jacobs tale of married life, jealousy, and riverside talk.
10734-a-collection-of-old-english-plays-:
A. H. Bullen's third volume of A Collection of Old English Plays, issued between 1882 and 1889, continues his rescue of forgotten Elizabethan and Jacobean drama. One play in the volume is printed here for the first time, and the others had not been reprinted before. Bullen thanks friends who lent rare books and read proofs for the edition.

His preface admits a setback: a promised play by Heywood could not be transcribed from its difficult handwriting, and must wait for a fourth volume. The plays that did appear reward readers with fresh plots and period verse. Students of early English drama will find here texts Bullen saved from obscurity.
10783-self-help-sailor-s-knots-part-3:
W. W. Jacobs's "Self-Help," the third tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, finds the night-watchman brooding over a sore toe and a touch of liver. He blames the landlord of the Queen's Head and the waterman who rapped his tender foot with an oar. Doing a man a kindness, he grumbles, only earns a blow years later.

The story turns that grievance into comedy, as the watchman recalls the kindness and its ungrateful reward. Jacobs's humor lies in the grumble itself, told in Thames-side dialect. Readers get a brief, funny monologue, complete on its own, from one of Jacobs's most durable characters.
1102-king-henry-vi-part-3:
William Shakespeare's third Henry VI play plunges into open civil war, as York and Lancaster tear England apart for the crown. Battles at Wakefield, Towton, and Tewkesbury claim lords and princes, while the ruthless Richard of Gloucester rises through murder toward the throne he will seize in the next play.

Henry, a pious king unfit for war, watches his realm bleed and longs for a shepherd's life. The play's violence is stark and its pace is swift. It closes the trilogy with the house of York triumphant and Richard waiting in the wings, a villain made ready.
11183-the-nest-egg-captains-all-book-3:
In this Captains All story, the night-watchman warns that sudden cleverness rarely pays, then tells of Charlie Tagg, a steady young sailor saving for marriage. Tagg's nest egg draws schemers, and his attempts to protect it tangle him in tricks that backfire one after another. Jacobs lets the watchman interrupt himself, correct himself, and savor each turn, so the telling matters as much as the plot.

The tale's comedy comes from ordinary greed meeting ordinary cunning, with neither side quite smart enough to win cleanly. Dialect carries the humor, and the waterfront setting keeps it grounded. It stands alone well, though it gains flavor beside the other Captains All yarns.
11473-made-to-measure-deep-waters-part-3:
Mr. Mott, a lonely older man in a quiet town, meets his niece Miss Garland at the station, proud of the pretty, well-dressed girl from London. She says she is tired of London and likes the peace of the little town, and he hopes she will stay a long time.

The comedy grows from a jilted lover, Mr. Hurst, and Mott's blunt view that high spirit is born, not made. Jacobs keeps the talk plain and the scene small: a front room, tea cups, and a family matter settled, or unsettled, by pride and plain speaking.
11509-the-life-of-jesus-christ-for-the-y:
Richard Newton's third volume for young readers covers the later ministry of Jesus, from the choosing of the apostles through teaching by parables and miracles to the Last Supper. Chapters take up liberality, humility, and little children, with the Transfiguration and lessons from Olivet to follow.

Pictures number the scenes in order, from the woman of Canaan and Peter's faith to Lazarus raised after four days dead. Zacchaeus the publican, Bartimaeus given sight, and the entry into Jerusalem appear in turn. Short tales drive each lesson home in plain words, such as a fine rod that catches no fish while a boy's poor rod succeeds.
11949-master-tales-of-mystery-volume-3:
Francis J. Reynolds collected and arranged this third volume of Master Tales of Mystery, drawing on popular detective and adventure writers. Arthur B. Reeve contributes The Poisoned Pen, The Invisible Rat, The Silent Bullet, The Deadly Tubs, The Black Hand, and The Steel Door, a run of scientific-detective stories.

Paul L. Ford's Great K. and A. Train Robbery, Max Pemberton's The Risen Dead, George Barr McCutcheon's Cowardice Court, and Burton E. Stevenson's Case of Mrs. Magnus follow, with Joseph Ernest's Episode, or The Black Casquette, among others. The anthology preserves the mystery story as readers of the early twentieth century knew it: ingenious crimes, bold criminals, and detectives working by observation and reason.
11953-a-popular-history-of-france-from-t:
Guizot's third volume of his History of France carries the narrative through the Hundred Years' War and into the Italian wars. Chapters treat Charles VI and the dukes of Burgundy, Charles VII and Joan of Arc from 1422 to 1461. Louis XI from 1461 to 1483, with a frontispiece of the Hôtel de Ville at Bourges.

The Italian campaigns follow, under Charles VIII from 1483 to 1498 and Louis XII from 1498 onward, as French kings carried their rivalries across the Alps. Guizot keeps his focus on kingship, war, and national formation, presenting Joan of Arc not as an isolated marvel but as part of a long struggle over who would rule France.
11973-dialstone-lane-part-3:
Part 3 of W. W. Jacobs's Dialstone Lane opens with church bells ringing for morning service, as Mr. Vickers, back from a stroll with Mr. William Russell and a couple of ferrets, returns home to breakfast. Contrary to custom, the small front room and kitchen are both empty. Breakfast, apart from a cold herring and the bitter remains of a pot of tea, has been cleared away.

This middle portion follows the treasure-hunt comedy into domestic confusion, as characters vanish, return, and misunderstand one another in Jacobs's seaside town. Ferrets, cold herrings, and cleared tables give the farce its texture, while the map and the expedition wait in the background for the later parts to resolve.
12123-bill-s-paper-chase-lady-of-the-bar:
Part 3 of Jacobs's Lady of the Barge stories, Bill's Paper Chase, opens with the night watchman reflecting on sailormen. He notes that they have their faults, though being close with their money is seldom one of them. The watchman recalls saving two golden sovereigns, thanks to a hole in his pocket, and sleeping rough before he got another ship.

Bill's paper chase follows a sailor's pursuit of money, papers, and a debtor through docks and lodgings, with Jacobs's usual irony: the chaser is as muddled as the chased. The story's humor lies in its vernacular voice, as the night watchman tells a tale of thrift and bad luck about the small sums that loom large in a sailor's life.
12153-the-understudy-night-watches-part-:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this short story for Night Watches, his Thames-side collection of 1911. As in the other tales, a night watchman narrates, in rough dockside speech, a yarn about sailors ashore and the trouble that follows them.

Sam Small, Ginger Dick, and Peter Russet pick up a stray black dog in a Commercial Road pub and, feeling sorry for it, smuggle it past its owner. Feeding it, hiding it, and dodging its real master fill the tale with small frauds that grow harder to sustain. The comedy lies in three men who pride themselves on kindness while breaking every rule to keep the dog. It ends as Jacobs tales often do, with the scheme undone by its own weight.
12203-blundell-s-improvement-odd-craft-p:
Venia Turnbull enjoys herself quietly in Blundell Improvement, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. From her seat by a farm window, she watches her father, kept from his Sunday nap by two admirers, struggle to stay polite.

The admirers compete for Venia hand, and Blundell, the farmer, must manage them without giving offense or losing his rest. The improvement of the title is a scheme, hatched by one suitor, to better his standing with father and daughter alike. Jacobs keeps the comedy rural and gentle: bees hum at the window, manners strain, and love proceeds by small stratagems. The story shows his gift for turning a Sunday afternoon call into a full farce.
1383-poems-volume-3:
George Meredith's third volume of poems gathers his later verse. The lyrics and sequences come from his maturity, when his thought on love, fate, and nature had deepened and his style had grown more compressed. The poems carry his familiar themes to a graver pitch.

Meredith writes with a philosopher's density and a poet's eye, and the volume rewards slow reading. It completes the arc begun in the first volume. The book suits readers who follow Meredith through his whole poetic career. The later lyrics show Meredith's thought grown graver and deeper.
1502-king-henry-vi-part-3:
The third part of Henry VI carries the Wars of the Roses to their bloodiest pitch, as York and Lancaster fight for the crown across English fields. Richard, Duke of York, claims the throne, his sons Edward and Richard press the claim, and battles at Towton and Tewkesbury decide the fate of kings.

Henry himself drifts through the slaughter, a gentle king unfit for civil war, while Margaret of Anjou fights fiercely for her son. The play ends with Edward on the throne and Richard of Gloucester already eyeing it. It is a grim, fast-moving chronicle of ambition and revenge.
15183-the-tragedy-of-the-chain-pier-ever:
Charlotte Braeme's Brighton tale, number three in the Everyday Life Library, opens by praising the West Pier over the older chain pier. Fashionable visitors crowd its shops, library, music rooms, and promenade, with white sails and tall town houses shining beyond. The scene sets up a story of love and loss by the sea.

Against that bright resort backdrop, Braeme builds a tragedy of hopes raised and broken, in her familiar melodramatic manner. Brighton itself acts as a character, gay on the surface and cruel underneath. Readers of Victorian sensation novels will find the pier, the crowds, and the heartbreak vividly drawn.
15537-the-reign-of-henry-the-eighth-volu:
James Anthony Froude's history of Henry VIII appears here in its first volume, with an introduction by W. Llewelyn Williams, published by Dent in London and Toronto and Dutton in New York. A Carlyle epigraph calls history the true epic poem and universal divine scripture. Seven chapters carry this volume, with notes.

Froude opens with the social condition of England in the sixteenth century. He warns that modern readers, used to daily change, struggle to enter a world that grew for centuries on a single type. Later chapters follow Wolsey's last years, the Parliament of 1529, church and state, Henry's marriage to Anne Boleyn, the Protestants, and last efforts of diplomacy. The history is vivid and partisan, and it shaped how generations pictured the English Reformation.
15876-the-unpopular-review-volume-ii-num:
The Unpopular Review for July to September 1914, volume two, number three, published quarterly in New York by Henry Holt and Company. The Review prided itself on unfashionable opinion, with editors and guests writing against the grain. Contents range across economics, politics, and culture. The tone is sharp, learned, and contrarian.

A. S. Johnson writes on unsocial investments, Hugh H. Lusk on an experiment in syndicalism, and Arthur J. Todd on labour, true demand, and immigrant supply. Fabian Franklin takes readers to Flatland, while David McGregor Means treats the disfranchisement of property. Clayton Hamilton, Paul Elmer More, and others complete the number. The issue captures 1914 debate before the war changed it.
16847-hinduism-and-buddhism-an-historica:
Sir Charles Eliot wrote this third volume of a historical sketch of Hinduism and Buddhism, following volumes one and two. The preface to volume one, reprinted here, explains his way of writing Asian words in Latin letters. He uses Wade's system for Chinese, the Pali Text Society system for Pali, and Monier-Williams for Sanskrit. Each tongue keeps its own standard form.

Eliot traces the two faiths across Asia, with care for names, texts, and local forms. The volume gives a broad, scholarly survey, not a sectarian plea. Readers who want a solid older history of Hindu and Buddhist thought, art, and spread will find it clear, learned, and still useful as a first map of a vast topic.
1707-a-history-of-science-volume-3:
Henry Smith Williams continues his history with the modern physical sciences, picking up after Newton and following astronomy, physics, and related fields into the nineteenth century. Halley and Hevelius, the transit of Mercury, and the slow work of measuring the planets open the volume.

Later chapters weigh how naturalists read the fossil record, with Cuvier's work on extinct animals given a central place. The book's method is the same as the earlier volumes: short chapters, named workers, and a plain account of what each generation added. A reader can follow science growing from Newton's laws toward the modern picture of earth and sky.
17376-the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-vol:
This third volume of the works of Guy de Maupassant, published in New York in 1909, gathers short stories under the title The Viaticum and Other Stories. The contents list runs from The Viaticum, The Relics, The Thief, and A Rupture. It moves through A Useful House, The Accent, Ghosts, and Crash, to An Honest Ideal and Stable Perfume. The Ill-Omened Groom, An Exotic Prince, Delila, Bertha, and A Night in Whitechapel follow.

Maupassant's tales are short, sharp, and often ironic, turning on a single twist or a revealed motive. Readers get the French master of the short story in English dress, at his most varied. The volume works as an introduction to Maupassant for newcomers and as a handy shelf copy for old admirers.
17723-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-:
Dated August 1885, this third number of the Bay State Monthly's third volume leads with a life of John Albion Andrew, the war governor of Massachusetts. Born in 1818 at Windham, Maine, Andrew rose from a small-town home to lead his state through the Civil War years.

The piece traces his youth, his home life, and the firm, kind temper that made him a trusted public man. The rest of the issue runs its usual mix of history and serial fiction. Readers meet a governor praised for nerve and heart, and they get a taste of how Boston magazines honored their heroes. It is a warm, old-style profile, rich in local pride.
17775-mrs-whittelsey-s-magazine-for-moth:
Mrs. A. G. Whittelsey edited this magazine for mothers and daughters, volume three, published in New York in 1852 by Henry M. Whittelsey of Nassau Street. Its motto, from the Bible, wishes sons grown as plants in youth and daughters as corner stones polished after the similitude of a palace. The volume was entered for copyright in 1852.

As a year's magazine, it mixes stories, advice, and devotional reading for mothers and their daughters. Readers get a mid-nineteenth-century family magazine, earnest, domestic, and moral in tone. The volume suits readers of women's periodicals and of American home life in the 1850s.
18804-prose-masterpieces-from-modern-ess:
This third volume of prose masterpieces gathers five Victorian essayists in one Putnam collection of 1891. James Anthony Froude opens with his Royal Institution lecture of February 1864 on the science of history, doubting whether past events, known only through books, can ever yield a true science.

Edward A. Freeman follows on race and language, William Ewart Gladstone on kin beyond sea, John Henry Newman on private judgment, and Leslie Stephen with an apology for plain speaking. Together the essays show leading minds of the age testing history, nationhood, faith, and frank speech in public argument. The volume suits readers who want strong Victorian prose on large questions, without the frame of a single author's book.
19976-the-mabinogion-vol-3:
Lady Charlotte Guest translated The Mabinogion from medieval Welsh. Volume three is credited to her directly in this edition. It opens with Pwyll, prince of Dyved, lord of its seven cantrevs. Pwyll is at Narberth, his chief palace, one famous day. He is minded to go hunting in Glyn Cuch. That hunt begins the First Branch of the Mabinogi. Its wonders include a stolen child and a lady on a white horse.

Guest's eleven tales made Welsh literature world property. Pwyll's branch sets the pattern: courtesy, magic, and slow justice. Rhiannon, the lady of the hunt, dominates its memory. The translation's Victorian grace can soften the Welsh edge. Still, the strangeness survives triumphantly. Volume three holds the cycle's heart.
20828-traditions-of-the-north-american-i:
Verse of deer in battle and moose in race opens volume three of the Indian traditions. Panthers, lakes, and a white canoe crowd the lines with wild images. Woe waits the red man cast by fate in a midnight swamp, the poem warns.

Poems and tales close James Athearn Jones's three-volume set of native lore. Songs of war, love, and spirits round out the camp-fire store. The set aimed to save a fading oral world for print readers. Modern readers must sift its period flaws, yet its pages still hold early, earnest records of stories that tribes prized and passed down.
2093-the-writings-of-samuel-adams-volume:
Harry Alonzo Cushing edits the third volume of Samuel Adams's writings, covering the middle years of the Revolution, when protest turned to war and independence. Letters and papers show Adams organising resistance. Adams's third volume covers the years when Congress moved toward independence.

The volume bridges the second volume's early resistance and the fourth volume's later republic, giving Adams at the height of his powers. Historians value it as a direct source for the patriot movement's inner work. Cushing's editing, with dates and notes, helps readers place each letter in the crisis.
21262-the-works-of-christopher-marlowe-v:
A. H. Bullen's three-volume edition of Christopher Marlowe closes with this third volume, published in London in 1885. It gathers Marlowe's poems rather than his plays: Hero and Leander first, then his translations of Ovid's Elegies and the first book of Lucan. The Passionate Shepherd to His Love, the lyric everyone knows, stands near the end.

Epigrams by John Davies, fragments, and a dialogue in verse fill out the volume, with appendices and an index to the notes. Two editions of Hero and Leander appeared in 1598, one with only Marlowe's part. Bullen's edition helped fix Marlowe's standing as a poet beside his fame as a dramatist.
2149-the-works-of-edgar-allan-poe-volume:
This third volume of Poe's works in the Raven Edition pairs his long sea narrative, The Narrative of A. Gordon Pym, with shorter tales including Ligeia, Morella, and King Pest. Pym's voyage to the South Seas opens the book. Pym, Poe's only novel, breaks off in mystery, a fact that has puzzled readers ever since.

Notes to the volume follow the tales, and the shorter pieces show Poe's range, from horror and beauty to satire and puzzle. The collection suits readers who want Poe beyond the famous poems, in the prose that made his name. Ligeia and Morella, tales of dead wives who return, show Poe's haunting, musical prose.
2169-miscellaneous-writings-and-speeches:
Macaulay's third volume of miscellaneous writings gathers his contributions to the Encyclopaedia Britannica, with poems, inscriptions, and translations. Atterbury, Bunyan, Goldsmith, Johnson, and Pitt receive full biographical essays. The Britannica essays, written in the 1850s, show Macaulay at his biographical best.

Shorter pieces follow, from an epitaph on Henry Martyn to a radical war song, the Battle of Naseby, and a translation of Dies Irae. The volume shows Macaulay the encyclopaedist at his clearest, judging lives and letters with vigour. His Johnson and Pitt pieces, in particular, mix life, letters, and political judgment.
21811-the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-3:
Lord Byron's narrative poems fill this third volume of his works, in an edition rich with notes by editor E. H. Coleridge. The Giaour and The Bride of Abydos stand among the poems here, tales of the Levant that made Byron famous across Europe. Coleridge prints deleted lines and variant readings from Byron's own manuscripts. Byron's footnotes stand beside the editor's, marked so readers can tell them apart.

These poems mix romance, guilt, and wild eastern scenery in Byron's swift, glowing verse. They were the sensation of their years, and their heroes gave English the word Byronic. The heavy notes suit the volume to study as well as pleasure. It is Byron with his workshop doors open, drafts and all.
2256-king-henry-vi-part-3:
The Wars of the Roses reach their bloodiest phase as Yorkists and Lancastrians trade crowns, betrayals, and battlefield murders. Part 3 opens with Henry VI's humiliating bargain, follows Edward IV's rise, and ends with the birth of Richard's ambition and the death of the young Prince Edward. Shakespeare piles atrocity on atrocity with grim energy.

A father killing his son and a son killing his father, unknowing, gives the play its most famous horror. Margaret of Anjou, fierce and grieving, dominates the Lancastrian cause. The sequence closes with England exhausted and a tyrant waiting in the wings.
22591-a-political-history-of-the-state-o:
A Political History of the State of New York is a three-volume history issued by Henry Holt and Company in 1906. The catalog record credits the publisher rather than a personal author. New York's politics, from colonial days onward, shaped the nation far beyond the state's borders, and this work traces that story in detail.

The sample opens at the birth of the state, as the second Continental Congress in May 1776 urged colonies without sound governments to form new ones fit for war. New York's patriot government, the writer notes, had not wholly satisfied its people. From that shaky start the volumes follow parties, leaders, and elections. Students of American political history will find a full period account of the Empire State's public life.
23666-mission-furniture-how-to-make-it-p:
This 1912 handbook from Popular Mechanics, edited by H. H. Windsor, is the third part of a practical series on making mission-style furniture at home. Written, as the series promised, so that readers can understand it, it gives measured plans for pieces a home workman could build from mill-planed, sanded stock cut to length.

The contents run from a piano bench and library table to a princess dresser, sewing box, fern stand, and wardrobe. Oak tables, a leather-back armchair, and a quarter-sawed oak settee follow, with notes on finishes and joints. For modern woodworkers and fans of the Craftsman style, it remains a usable pattern book from the height of the mission fashion.
23748-history-of-the-united-states-volum:
E. Benjamin Andrews, president of Brown University, wrote this third volume of his History of the United States, published by Scribner's in 1896 with four hundred illustrations and maps. The volume covers Period Two, from 1814 to 1840, when Whigs and Democrats contended until the slavery controversy came to dominate American politics.

Chapters treat the Whig party and its mission, the tariff, the Bank, and internal improvements, with portraits of Adams, Webster, and Clay. Florida and the Monroe Doctrine get a chapter of their own. Andrews writes for general readers, and the volume's frontispiece, the first gun fired from Fort Sumter, points ahead to the storm this period was brewing.
24940-the-nursery-september-1873-vol-xiv:
The Nursery for September 1873, volume fourteen, number three, continues Shorey's Boston monthly for youngest readers. Its prose runs from The Queer Things That Happened to Nelly and The Six Ducks to Rambles in the Woods. What I Saw at the Seashore follows, with verse and music beside them.

Nelly Burton, tired from weeding all summer morning, wishes for fine clothes and no work, and strange things follow. In the woods, Paul teaches Rachel about sweet-smelling plants: wintergreen for soap and candy, and sassafras bark, red like cinnamon, for beer and soaps. The issue mixes wonder tales with plain nature lessons for small children.
2551-droll-stories-volume-3:
Honore de Balzac gathered these tales from the abbeys of Touraine, and this third volume holds the third ten stories. A prologue sets the tone, then monks, wives, judges, and poor men trade tricks in tales of love, lust, and sharp revenge.

Bertha the penitent, the pretty maid of Portillon who outwits her judge, and the monk Amador, glorious abbot of Turpenay, lead a bawdy parade. Balzac writes in a mock old French style, full of jest and earthy humor. The stories are frank, funny, and far from polite, and they show his comic side at full stretch.
2580-the-french-revolution-volume-3:
Hippolyte Taine closes his French Revolution trilogy with the establishment of the revolutionary government. This fourth volume of his Origins of Contemporary France follows the Jacobin regime as it hardens into a system of rule, with its committees, courts, and armies.

Taine studies how terror became policy, and how the new rulers justified coercion in the name of the people. His sources are dense, his tone unsparing, and his argument clear: revolution, once armed, builds its own despotism. The volume completes a history that still divides readers and historians alike.
25889-washington-and-the-american-republ:
Benson J. Lossing carries his life of Washington and the young republic into a third volume, printed in New York in 1870. Lossing, known for his pictorial histories of the Civil War and the Revolution, follows Washington through the trials of the presidency. Even wide fame could not shield his acts from fierce party attack. A proclamation draws fire as a royal edict and a daring stretch of executive power.

The volume's twenty six chapters track the cabinet, the press, and the public mood. Jefferson's reluctant vote and the rage of foes stand out, foes who called the move partial to England and hostile to France. Portraits and scenes break the text. The book gives a full, plain account of how Washington bore praise and blame alike in the first years of the republic.
25890-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-april-18:
Joseph Rodes Buchanan edits this April 1887 number of his Journal of Man, a magazine of psychometry, anthropology, and reform. The contents list psychometry as the divine science, a modern miracle worker, human longevity, and justice to the Indians by John Beeson. Short notes take up the brain, mesmeric cures, medical despotism, the dangerous classes, arbitration, and quakes and predictions.

Buchanan claims psychometry holds imperial rank among sciences, since it guides and controls human affairs like kings, statesmen, and saints. A note on Henry Ward Beecher blames his fatal stroke on a life of strain and scorned prudence, and says magnetic treatment might have saved him. Beeson's piece recalls President Grant placing Indian affairs under church control. The number is a bold, odd record of fringe science in the late nineteenth century.
2596-the-forsyte-saga-volume-3:
John Galsworthy closes the Forsyte saga in this volume, joining Awakening and To Let. Jon Forsyte and Fleur Forsyte, children of the old feud, meet at Robin Hill, and their love revives the quarrel their fathers could never settle.

To Let follows mothers and sons, fathers and daughters, through meetings in Green Street and country idylls, toward a parting that feels fated. Galsworthy writes with elegiac grace about beauty, possession, and youth slipping away. The volume ends the saga on a note of loss, and it remains its most tender book.
2621-the-home-book-of-verse-volume-3:
Burton Egbert Stevenson compiled this third volume of The Home Book of Verse, drawing on the same wide anthology as its companions. Poems of youth and age return, with Keats on the human seasons and verses for babies by Barr, Spofford, Blake, and MacDonald.

The set favors poems that sing well aloud and stay in the memory, from nursery tenderness to meditations on growing old. Stevenson chose for households, not classrooms, and the book invites browsing. Readers will find a generous shelf of English verse, arranged for comfort rather than chronology.
2673-the-complete-writings-of-charles-du:
Charles Dudley Warner's third volume of complete writings opens in the wilderness, with a plain account of killing a bear in the Adirondacks. So many conflicting stories had spread, Warner says, that justice to the public, himself, and the bear required the facts.

How Spring Came in New England, Captain John Smith, and Pocahontas follow, mixing nature writing with history and humor. Warner writes as a companionable traveler, fond of woods, rivers, and old tales. The volume shows his range, from a bear hunt to the founding of Virginia. Bear, spring, and founding history sit side by side here.
27597-the-english-utilitarians-volume-1-:
Leslie Stephen published this first volume of The English Utilitarians with Duckworth in London in 1900. He treats men who shaped English thought and political action across three generations.

Bentham, James Mill, and John Stuart Mill led them in turn, and Stephen speaks of each. This volume opens with political conditions, the industrial spirit, and social problems, from pauperism and education to the slave-trade and the French Revolution. It then treats philosophy, Bentham's life, and Bentham's doctrine, from first principles and the panopticon to codification and radicalism. A note on Bentham's writings closes the volume.
27647-the-economist-volume-1-no-3:
The Economist, or the Political, Commercial, Agricultural, and Free-Trade Journal, published this third number on Saturday, 16 September 1843, at sixpence. Its epigraph, from Burke, warns against shrinking concerns to the dimensions of small minds.

Contents include our Brazilian trade and the anti-slavery party, the fallacy of protection, and agriculture, with court and aristocracy and music and musicales. The metropolis, the provinces, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales follow, with foreign news from France, Spain, Austria and Italy, Turkey, and Egypt. The United States, Canada, and the colonies appear too, with emigration during the last seventeen years and correspondence. Free trade closes the number.
28046-critical-and-historical-essays-vol:
Lord Macaulay's Critical and Historical Essays, volume three of three, gathers long review essays first printed in the Edinburgh Review. The 1899 Riverside Press edition opens with Ranke's History of the Popes, praised for fair, wide learning, and moves on to Leigh Hunt, Lord Holland, and Warren Hastings.

Later essays treat Frederick the Great, Madame d'Arblay, Addison, Barere, and the Earl of Chatham. Macaulay judges books by their facts, their style, and their sense of the past, and he writes with great force and confidence. The volume gives a strong sample of Victorian criticism at its most readable.
2881-the-legends-of-the-jews-volume-3:
Louis Ginzberg's third volume of The Legends of the Jews, translated from the German manuscript by Paul Radin, covers the Exodus to the death of Moses. Ginzberg dedicates it to his mother on her seventieth birthday and frames the period as the birth of Israel as a nation. Moses appears as both the greatest religious guide and the first national leader, described as the wisest of the wise. The legends fill the desert years with wonders.

Storehouses of snow and hail stand beside angels of burning flame, and a sea of ice hangs above fiery creatures no mortal could cross in less than five hundred years. The volume gathers these traditions into a continuous narrative. It serves readers who want the Exodus story as later Jewish imagination retold it.
29403-the-esperantist-vol-1-no-3:
Number three of The Esperantist, dated January 1904 and edited by H. Bolingbroke Mudie, served as the Esperanto gazette for spreading the new international language. Published by the Esperanto Club of London at fourpence a copy, it urged readers to form local groups and write to the club's honorary secretary. Its contents mix movement news with literature in and about Esperanto.

Inside are editor's notes, a piece on radium by Sir William Ramsay, two fables, nursery rhymes by Ben Elmy, a story called A Terrible Night, and translations of The Tempest and Casabianca. The mix shows a young movement eager to prove its tongue could carry science, verse, and drama. Students of planned languages will find a lively snapshot of Esperanto in its early years.
30754-the-stones-of-venice-volume-1-of-3:
John Ruskin's first volume of The Stones of Venice, called The Foundations, opens his great study of Venetian building. The volume sits in the Library Edition of Ruskin's complete works, and its front shows Venice from a painting by J. M. W. Turner. Ruskin says in his preface that he set aside much he had meant to say there, since the book had been advertised for a year and a half.

Chapters begin with the quarry, the virtues of architecture, and the six divisions of architecture, then move through wall base, wall veil, wall cornice, pier base, and shaft. Ruskin teaches readers to see a building from its stone upward, judging craft, truth, and beauty as one. It is the groundwork for the later volumes on Byzantine, Gothic, and Renaissance Venice, and a classic of art criticism.
30755-the-stones-of-venice-volume-2-of-3:
John Ruskin's second volume of The Stones of Venice closes his account of the city's old buildings, after a plan that grew from two volumes to three. This volume is called The Sea Stories, and it takes the Byzantine period first, then the Gothic period. Its chapters move from Torcello and Murano to St. Mark's, the Byzantine palaces, the nature of Gothic building, and the Ducal Palace.

Ruskin writes as both a critic and a guide, judging stonework, carving, and design while pointing readers to what to look at in churches and palaces. Notes on pictures, tides, dress, and old inscriptions sit in the back, and a third volume was to hold the later Renaissance work and a full index. Readers who love Venice, art, or old craft will find a rich, opinionated survey of a city built on water.
30756-the-stones-of-venice-volume-3-of-3:
John Ruskin's third volume of The Stones of Venice, called The Fall, closes his study of the city's architecture. It sits in the Library Edition of Ruskin's complete works, with the Bridge of Sighs on its front. It also holds the index for all three volumes, with links in the electronic version. This volume turns from the early city to its later decline.

Its chapters cover the third, or Renaissance, period in three parts: Early Renaissance, Roman Renaissance, and Grotesque Renaissance, ending with a conclusion. Appendices treat the architect of the Ducal Palace, the theology of Spenser, Austrian rule in Italy, and the dates of palaces. Ruskin judges Renaissance Venice with severity and love together, and the volume rewards readers who have followed his argument from the foundations.
31078-curiosities-of-literature-vol-3:
Volume three of Isaac Disraeli's Curiosities of Literature, in the new edition edited with memoir and notes by his son, the Earl of Beaconsfield, gathers dozens of short essays. They treat books and their makers. Entries take up masques, the history of new words, the philosophy of proverbs, political nicknames, and the building of Blenheim. They also tell the secret history of Sir Walter Raleigh, including an account of his last hours.

Other pieces treat literary forgeries, Lord Bacon at home, the death of Queen Elizabeth, the dictionary of Trévoux, and the pearl Bibles with six thousand errata. Anecdotal, learned, and endlessly quotable, the volume remains a browser's delight for anyone who loves the byways of literary history.
31095-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Volume three of Stories by American Authors, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1896, collects six magazine stories. Lucretia P. Hale opens with The Spider's Eye, in which a visitor alone in a theatre wonders whether a room built to carry every stage whisper might also carry whispers back. That makes one listener the center of all information.

Frances Hodgson Burnett follows with a story of the Latin Quarter, George Parsons Lathrop with Two Purse-Companions, David D. Lloyd with Poor Ogla-Moga, Celia Thaxter with A Memorable Murder, and Brander Matthews with Venetian Glass. Together they sample the range of American short fiction in the 1880s, from comedy to mystery and romance.
31645-the-tatler-volume-3:
The Tatler, volume three, edited with introduction and notes by George A. Aitken, author of The Life of Richard Steele, was published in New York by Hadley and Mathews. Aitken's edition runs to four volumes, and this third volume continues the great early eighteenth-century periodical. The Tatler, founded by Steele with Addison, mixed essays, news, and social comment, and invented the periodical essay as English readers know it.

Aitken's notes identify persons, places, and allusions, making the Tatler readable for modern students. Readers of eighteenth-century literature will find in this volume the daily life of London in Queen Anne's reign: coffee houses, theaters, fashions, and follies, observed with wit. The edition is a scholarly standard, still useful for anyone reading Steele and Addison.
31823-the-orpheus-c-kerr-papers-series-3:
Robert H. Newell's third series of the Orpheus C. Kerr Papers, published in New York by Carleton in 1865, gathers the wit and sarcasm that made Newell famous in the Civil War years. A publisher's notice says the papers are now comprised in three volumes, uniformly bound at $1.50 each, and that their circulation in book form has been enormous.

The volume opens with a French anecdote about Louvois, Sully, and an appointment won by impudence, before turning to memoirs of the opera and Newell's Civil War satire. Readers get a classic of American wartime humor, mocking generals, politicians, and the press with a pen name that became a household word.
32357-lulu-s-library-volume-2-of-3:
Louisa M. Alcott's Lulu's Library, volume two of three, was published in Boston by Little, Brown, and Company in 1901, copyright 1887. Alcott inscribed it to Ellen T. Emerson, praised as a good fairy still among us, loved by poets and children. Its stories run from The Frost King and How the Fairies Conquered Him through Lilybell and Thistledown, Ripple the Water Sprite, and Eva's Visit to Fairyland.

Sunshine and Her Brothers and Sisters, The Fairy Spring, Queen Aster, The Brownie and the Princess, Mermaids, Little Bud, and The Flower's Story complete the volume. Alcott's preface explains that she wrote most of these stories at sixteen for her younger sisters and their playmates, the little Emersons and Channings. Years on, they came out again as Flower Fables. Enlarged, they were reissued to delight the children of those children. Readers get Alcott fairy stories.
32377-a-struggle-for-rome-v-3:
Felix Dahn's historical novel reaches its third and final volume here, translated from German by Lily Wolffsohn. The trilogy follows Goths, Romans, and Byzantines in their struggle for Rome as an empire breaks apart and new powers fight over Italy. Leaders, soldiers, and families are caught between loyalty to a falling order and hope for a new one.

This closing volume carries the vast story toward its end, with battles, councils, and personal fates deciding who will hold Rome. Dahn writes on a grand scale, pairing political argument with romance and heroism. Readers who followed volumes one and two will find the long contest resolved here, in the same rich, dramatic manner.
32981-trevethlan-a-cornish-story-volume-:
William Davy Watson's Trevethlan opens in late September some thirty years earlier. It is the first volume of a three-volume Cornish story published in 1848, and Henry Trevethlan dies in the state bedchamber of Trevethlan Castle in Cornwall. The lofty room, lit by Gothic casements looking over the sea, sets a scene of fallen greatness. A Shakespeare epigraph warns that honor follows place, riches, and favor rather than merit alone.

From that deathbed the novel unfolds a family story of inheritance, pride, and fortune's turns in a Cornish setting. Watson, a barrister, writes with a lawyer's eye for wills, claims, and the weight of a name, while the castle and coast give the tale its gloom and grandeur. This first volume lays the ground for a long Victorian saga of a house in decline and the people caught in its fall.
33540-view-of-the-state-of-europe-during:
Henry Hallam's View of the State of Europe During the Middle Ages, volume three, in a new edition from London in 1860, completes his great survey. Its contents open with chapter eight, part three, on the English constitution, and move through the later Middle Ages with Hallam's learned, judicious prose. Hallam, a fellow of the Royal Society, writes for readers who want history as argument, not just story.

The volume's strength is its clear, systematic order, weighing institutions, laws, and peoples across centuries. Its tone is scholarly and calm, suited to students and general readers alike. For those who study medieval Europe, it remains a classic, if dated, guide to how the continent grew from feudalism to modern states.
33555-on-strike-till-3:
Grant Balfour, author of Canada My Home and other poems, tells a verse story of labor and hardship in this Toronto volume of 1913. The poem opens with a cottage beside a deep ravine, overlooking elm, willow, beech, and birch above a shaded stream. The poem moves into winter, when snow covers vale and heights in dazzling white. A lamp in the cottage window falls on sheets hung on lines, marking the woman's calling.

Christmas Eve brings a mother and her little boy David into focus, as work from dawn till dark earns poor reward. Balfour writes in the earnest, pictorial manner of Canadian popular verse, letting landscape and domestic detail carry the human cost of a strike. The poem is a short, affecting piece for readers interested in early Canadian labor literature.
3368-a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-3:
William Dean Howells carries A Hazard of New Fortunes into its third part with a banquet. The scheme to celebrate the initial success of Every Other Week expanded in Fulkerson's fancy into a series. Fulkerson drops the plan for a small supper in Mrs Leighton's parlors for staff, artists, and authors, and dreams up something far grander instead.

The modest parlor meal gives way to a Delmonico's dinner for the city's leading writers and artists. The expansion is the novel in miniature: ambition outrunning means, and a magazine's success spent before it is secure. Readers will enjoy Howells's comedy of promotion, where a celebration becomes a hazard all its own.
33694-tales-from-blackwood-volume-3:
William Blackwood and Sons gathered tales from Blackwood's Magazine in this third volume: A Reading Party in the Long Vacation, Father Tom and the Pope, and La Petite Madelaine by Mrs. Southey. They also include Bob Burke's Duel with Ensign Brady by William Maginn and The Headsman. These include A Tale of Doom, and The Wearyful Woman by John Galt. The opening tale, from Maga in August 1843, jokes about Oxford undergraduates who form joint-stock cramming companies for the long vacation.

Half a dozen young men take shares in a private tutor, pitch camp in a dull Welsh or seaside spot, and persuade themselves they are doing business. The other tales range from Irish comedy and French romance to duels, doom, and weary women. The collection captures Blackwood's wit, variety, and nineteenth-century magazine storytelling at its best.
3373-their-silver-wedding-journey-volume:
William Dean Howells closes the Marches' silver wedding journey in this third volume. When their train makes its first stop, a young German enters the Marches' compartment with a bow. His obvious struggle not to smoke prompts March to urge him to light a cigarette. The friendly overture led to talk, and the young man explained himself.

By trade he designs railways, works for the government on this very line, and rides its length on official business. The small encounter carries the volume's mood: Europe met in compartments, in talk, and in kindnesses between strangers. Readers finishing the trilogy's last journey will find the Marches older and wiser, and their marriage, like their train, still moving.
33802-the-mysteries-of-paris-illustrated:
Eugène Sue continues The Mysteries of Paris in this third volume, illustrated with etchings in the de luxe edition limited to one thousand copies. Fourteen chapters move from the Temple, where Rigolette and Rodolph walk through deep snow hardened by a sharp wind toward the immense and singular bazaar, through an arrest, Jacques Ferrand.

Later chapters follow Mont Saint-Jean, La Louve and La Goualeuse, a protectress, a forced friendship, and Cecily. Etchings show a head taken between hands, a sheet of paper drawn out, Morel fallen back on a stool, a scolding, a suicide, and La Goualeuse in prison. Sue deepens his portrait of Parisian crime, charity, and hidden identity, and the volume carries his great serial toward its middle revelations.
33988-to-win-the-love-he-sought-the-grea:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this third volume of The Great Awakening, published in New York in 1910 and 1912 by P. F. Collier and Son. The contents run from a meeting and a singer through treachery, a Marioni's oath, and a meeting of the Order, to Lord Lumley, Margharita's diary, white hyacinths, pine trees, and storms.

Oppenheim, author of The Mischief-Maker and Havoc, writes of love sought at great cost, with hate, fear, and a return to reason along the way. The volume closes a long romance of passion and intrigue. It offers a period tale of love pursued through darkness.
3648-the-dwelling-place-of-light-volume-:
This third volume of Winston Churchill's industrial novel follows Janet Bumpus as she listens to a labor speaker on Hampton Common. His phrases play on her emotions like music, and when his voice rises at the climax she feels like weeping. Around her, a large part of the common is black with people of sixteen nationalities, gathered on trampled snow in watery winter sunlight to listen wistfully.

Churchill borrows the method of the movies here, cutting from scene to scene as the town's workers gather. The volume follows Janet's political awakening amid strikes and mill town hardship. Readers who began the story in volume one will find its emotional center here, where a young woman hears her own hopes spoken aloud.
3683-mr-crewe-s-career-volume-3:
This third volume of Winston Churchill's political novel follows the reform campaign into its public phase. The reform rallies no longer resemble matinees, and two real reporters now accompany the campaign, while the State Tribune prints column reports of hearings. On a porch in Edmundton, the Honourable Adam Hunt smokes cigars, little heeding rising waters, as visitors bring him cheques for necessary expenses.

Churchill shows reform learning to fight: crowds, newspapers, and legislative hearings replace drawing room talk. The chapter called Blameless Life weighs Hunt's record against Crewe's hopes. Readers who followed the first volumes will find here the campaign's heat, where idealism meets the daily price of politics.
3738-a-far-country-volume-3:
Winston Churchill carries Hugh Paret into middle life in the third book of his novel of modern America. The city Hugh serves has grown rich fast, drawing immigrants and grand tourists alike, and its new millionaires are turned out almost weekly, so the tale goes. Hugh, now a power in business and politics, finds that success has cost him the very things he once prized, and his marriage bears the strain.

A painful scene with his wife Maude anchors the volume, as she tells him plainly that his career is all he truly cares for, while he begs her not to leave. Churchill keeps the focus on conscience rather than scandal, asking what a life of getting is worth once the getting is done. Readers who followed Hugh from boyhood will find this closing stretch the most searching part of the novel.
3840-memoirs-of-marguerite-de-valois-que:
This third volume leaves Marguerite's own memoirs behind and offers instead a history of the house of Valois. It opens with Charles, Count of Valois, younger brother of Philip the Fair, and traces the succession crisis after three kings died without sons. The twelve peers held that the crown could never pass to a woman or through a woman. So the baby daughter of Charles the Fourth was set aside, and Philip of Valois took the throne.

Later chapters follow the new house through Italian wars. French armies forced their way home in 1496, and a king ruined by debauchery still won his people's love by kindness and late reforms. Louis of Orleans succeeded him as Louis the Twelfth in 1498. Readers who want the background to Marguerite's story will find a compact dynastic history, plainly told.
3849-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
Madame de Montespan's third book centers on the strangest love affair at court, between the Marquis de Lauzun and the Grande Mademoiselle de Montpensier. Lauzun, noticing a kindly glance, plays the fascinating suitor day by day until the proud princess, giving up her noble indifference, falls madly in love with a schemer who despised her. Held back by pride and etiquette, she at last presses a written offer of marriage into his hand in a recess.

The king settles a secret union, then sends Lauzun to Pignerol, where the princess's liberality supports him in a strange fashion. A later passage has Mademoiselle scolding a widowed prince who sought her wealth, reminding him that his lovely wife was poisoned on his watch. The volume is Montespan at her most theatrical, with love, pride, and revenge in full dress.
3929-prince-zilah-volume-3:
Jules Claretie's third volume of Prince Zilah turns on pardon, punishment, and a packet of letters. A cry escapes Zilah in accents of pain that strike Varhely like a knife, as the Prince exclaims that pardon must come before punishing, and names the other. Varhely clenches his fist with rage, thinking of the letters he held in his hands and might have destroyed had he known.

How is pardon possible while Menko lives, he asks himself, and no word more passes until they reach the villa. There Zilah shakes Varhely's hand, retires to his chamber, lights his lamp, and reads and rereads letters not addressed to him. Readers who like Claretie's melodrama will find a volume where honor, jealousy, and a secret correspondence collide.
3933-zibeline-volume-3:
Philippe de Massa's third volume of Zibeline turns to soldiers, honor, and Paris talk. Lenaieff asks a German captain whether he too has trodden the primrose path. The honest captain lays a large hand on his heart and swears he has never loved any woman but his own wife. That astonishes Parisians, he adds benevolently, and Lenaieff answers that quite the contrary assures them peace of mind.

Glasses clink a second time. Lenaieff tells Henri that the military governor has asked him to the review at Vincennes next day, where he will see Henri at the head of his division. The volume mixes camp comedy with society intrigue. Readers who like Massa's romances will find a book of oaths, toasts, and reputations defended over wine.
3937-a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-vol:
Andre Theuriet's third volume of A Woodland Queen turns inward to its heroine's wounded pride. Troubled waters run through her brain, and the dominant idea is that her self respect has been wounded. The shock to her maidenly modesty and the shame attending it affect her physically, as if she had been belittled and degraded by a personal stain, and the downfall causes deep humiliation.

By slow degrees, however, a faint germ of gladness crops up in her heart, and close examination finds its origin. She is now loosed from her obligations toward Claudet, and the prospect of being once more free affords immediate consolation. Readers who like Theuriet's woodland romance will find a volume of shame, release, and a heart learning its own freedom.
3941-the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-ce:
Alfred de Musset's third volume of The Confession of a Child of the Century deepens Octave's torment over Brigitte. After dinner she feels the air would do her good and asks whether they shall walk to the opera. Octave refuses to go, staying home while she takes Smith's arm and leaves. He remains alone all evening, paper before him, trying in vain to collect his thoughts for writing.

As a lonely lover draws a mistress's letter from his bosom and loses himself in reverie, so Octave shuts himself in solitude. He yields to the sweet allurement of doubt. Before him stand the two empty seats Brigitte and Smith just occupied, which he scrutinizes anxiously as if they could tell him something. Readers who like Musset's jealousy study will find a volume of watching, waiting, and self torture.
3945-monsieur-de-camors-volume-3:
Octave Feuillet's third volume of Monsieur de Camors turns on a wife's terrible revelation. A young countess tells Madame de Tecle, in a low voice and without once looking up, what has been revealed to her and confirmed by her husband's avowal. Madame de Tecle does not interrupt once during the cruel recital, and only imprints a kiss on her hair from time to time.

The countess, ashamed as if of another's crime, fears she has exaggerated her misfortune, since her mother receives the confidence with such calmness. But Madame de Tecle's calm is that of the martyrs, the narrator says, for all Christians suffered under the tiger's claws. Readers who like Feuillet's dramas of honor will find a volume of confession, shame, and maternal steadiness.
3949-cinq-mars-volume-3:
Alfred de Vigny's third volume of Cinq Mars pauses on a king surveying his battlefield. The cannon has ceased to roar when broken columns of infantry fall back into Perpignan, and the remainder already stands within the walls. On the plain no living man is seen save the glittering squadrons of the king, who follow him and form ranks as they go.

He returns at a slow walk and contemplates with satisfaction a field swept clear of enemies. He passes haughtily under the very fire of Spanish guns. They send only a few balls after him, whether from lack of skill, secret agreement with the prime minister, or shame at killing a king of France. Readers who like Vigny's history will find a volume of war, pride, and a monarch caught between minister and crown.
3956-l-abbe-constantin-volume-3:
Ludovic Halevy's third volume of L'Abbe Constantin turns on a young woman's heart and an older woman's reading of it. Susie guards her feelings as a miser guards and caresses the first coins of his treasure, waiting for the day she sees clearly into her own heart and is sure she loves. On that day she would speak, and how happy she would be to tell all to Susie herself, the narrator's confidante.

Mrs Scott, meanwhile, attributes Jean's growing melancholy to herself, flattered by the thought of being beloved and vexed at the same time. She holds Jean in great esteem and affection, but is distressed that his sadness might come from her, while Susie remains conscious of her own innocence. Readers who like Halevy's comedy will find a volume of misunderstanding, affection, and hearts not yet spoken.
3960-a-romance-of-youth-volume-3:
Paris in the late nineteenth century gives the backdrop for the third part of Francois Coppee's novel about a young poet named Amedee. The volume picks up his story after his first steps in print, when cafes and small journals begin to notice his work.

Amedee's sonnets win praise in La Guepe, and writers who meet at the Cafe de Seville start to talk about the rising poet. The chapters follow his growing fame, the friends and rivals it brings, and the strain that success puts on his hopes and his heart. Readers get a warm, street-level view of a young writer learning how praise, pride, and love can pull in different ways.
3965-cosmopolis-volume-3:
Paul Bourget's third volume of Cosmopolis turns from plot to the code of honor itself. The narrator asks how women can admit the inflexible rigor that founds manly relations, when they allow no similar rigor in their arguments with men or their discussions among themselves. Accustomed to appeal from convention to instinct and from reason to sentiment, women face laws of justice or honor in a state of incomprehension worse than ignorance.

A duel, for example, appears to them like an arbitrary drama, which the wish of one concerned can change at fancy. Ninety nine women out of a hundred would think like Lydia Maitland, the novel's American heroine, and treat a point of honor as a quarrel to be talked away. Readers who like Bourget's moral psychology will find a volume of duels, scruples, and two worlds misunderstanding each other.
3970-jacqueline-volume-3:
Th. Bentzon's novel reaches a darker turn in its third volume, as Jacqueline feels for the first time how poverty and a lack of protection expose her to insult. A man named Talbrun treats her as a plaything, and the slight cuts her pride deeply.

Jacqueline faces the hurt with a mix of anger and shame, asking what right any man has to use her so. Her womanly instincts rebel, yet she has few shields and fewer allies. The volume is the novel's painful middle passage, showing a young woman who must find her own strength when the adults around her fail to guard her.
3974-the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-volume-:
Rene Bazin's diary novel continues into summer in its third volume, with a fishing trip and the return of an old friend. A letter from Jupille gives minute directions for the meeting, and the diarist walks from Sceaux across woods toward the forts.

The July entries keep the book's easy mix of travel, talk, and study, as the young scholar steps out of his books into fields and water. Old ties renew and new plans take shape along the way. Readers get the warmest stretch of the novel so far, where nature and friendship offer a break from family pressure and scholarly worry.
3978-fromont-and-risler-volume-3:
Alphonse Daudet's third volume turns to Desiree, called Mam'zelle Zizi, whose mornings brighten when Frantz comes to sit at her feet as in old days. He no longer comes to talk of Sidonie, and the change gives her a quiet, daily joy.

Around that tender center, the novel keeps its Paris business world in motion, with the house of Fromont, its workers, and its tangled marriages. Daudet writes with warmth for the overlooked and sharp eyes for pride and gain. The volume offers a softer passage in a hard story, where small kindnesses count for a great deal.
3983-gerfaut-volume-3:
Charles de Bernard's novel deepens its central struggle in the third volume, as Madame de Bergenheim fights love with the help of falsehood. Virtue, doubting its own strength, turns to deceit as a shield, while Octave tries to stir her jealousy.

The volume is a study in defense and attack within a marriage-bound world, where honor demands concealment and feeling demands truth. Bernard follows each move with care, showing how a plan built on deceit can wound the very duty it means to guard. Readers who like courtly intrigue and moral tension will find this the novel's most tightly wound part.
3988-conscience-volume-3:
Hector Malot's novel tightens in its third volume around testimony and a doctor's attempt to shape it. Saniel insists on seeing Nougarede, not to falsify what Phillis said, but hoping his medical voice can show that a paralytic witness counts for no more than a confused one.

At the first words of excuse, Nougarede stops him, and the plan fails. Malot uses that blocked move to show how guilt narrows a man's choices, turning each clever step into a new trap. The volume keeps the crime story grounded in talk, sickrooms, and law, with Saniel's conscience pressing harder as the net draws close.
3993-madame-chrysantheme-volume-3:
Pierre Loti's Japan novel continues in its third volume aboard ship and ashore in late August. The Triomphante leaves its dock between the mountains and takes up old moorings in the harbor, under a clear sky swept clean as if by a cyclone.

Loti notes duty hours, harbor hills, and the strange clarity of light, keeping his sailor's eye on both ship routine and shore life. The volume carries the story of his brief Japanese marriage forward through festivals and farewells. Readers get vivid, firsthand scenes of a port world that feels at once near and far from home.
3998-an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-volum:
Emile Souvestre's Paris journal continues in its third volume into autumn, when nights grow cold and long and the sun no longer wakes the writer before work. Warm under his counterpane, he argues each morning between activity and idleness, waiting like the Gascon for the dispute to settle.

The volume keeps the journal's mix of season notes and short essays, this time turning to country, home, and the duties of a citizen. Souvestre writes from his attic perch with mild humor and plain sense. Readers get a calm, companionable book, best read a little at a time, like letters from a thoughtful neighbor.
4103-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's Mayflower history continues in its third volume with the officers and crew of the ship. The pilot John Clarke, hired by Weston and Cushman before a vessel was even found, holds the distinction of being the first man shipped for the voyage.

Ames traces each officer and sailor through records and inference, showing how much the Pilgrim venture owed to seamen as well as saints. The volume suits readers who like maritime detail, from hiring and wages to duties at sea. It adds the crew's story to the better-known tale of the passengers.
4259-andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-mili:
The third volume of John McElroy's prison narrative picks up inside the Andersonville stockade. Daily life there had settled into grim routine. Chapters describe the difficulty of exercise and the prison marketplace the men called the Rialto. They describe the cursing of the Confederacy and the battle of Spottsylvania Court House as told among prisoners.

McElroy's picture of the camp is unsparing. It shows a crowded mass of men with almost no movement in or out. Sickness and despair grow in that stillness. Read with the earlier volumes, this section shows how prisoners kept some order and talk alive.
4403-the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-e:
Book Three of George Meredith's Shaving of Shagpat opens on the enchanted sea, where a cockle-shell skims calmly, then pitches on surging foam. The surges boil like savage animals, hissing with anger, as Shibli Bagarag's voyage grows wilder. The lily of the enchanted sea gives the book its first tale.

Later tales tell of Noorna bin Noorka, the genie Karaz, and the princess of Oolb, with the wiles of Rabesqurat and the palace of Aklis. The sons of Aklis and the sword of Aklis complete the book. Meredith's nested fantasies carry Shibli closer to the blade that must shave Shagpat, through marvels told in ornate prose.
4408-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volum:
George Meredith's third volume of The Ordeal of Richard Feverel carries Richard's story into crisis. Its contents list a summons to town to hear a sermon, the approaches of fever, a crisis in the apple-disease, and the spring primrose and the autumnal. Later chapters record the hero taking a step, his rapid development, and an intercession for the heroine.

The volume opens with Berry, the baronet's man, arriving post-haste from town with orders to conduct Richard thither, and Richard refusing to go. Meredith follows the clash between father and son to its painful point. Readers of the first volumes will find the system's costs now fully counted, in a novel of growing tragic force.
4415-sandra-belloni-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni opens with Wilfrid leading a town life and visiting Stornley. He is not in love with Lady Charlotte Chillingworth, Meredith notes, but he is in harness to her. In love, one has some idea where one would go, while in harness one is pulled along with no say in where the road ends.

The book's chapters promise the return of the sentimentalist into bondage, life at Brookfield, and a walk by Wilming Weir. The return of Mr. Pericles, the pitfall of sentiment, and Wilfrid diplomatizing follow, with Emilia making a move and a farce within a farce. Emilia's singing career and Wilfrid's wavering heart drive the comedy.
4423-rhoda-fleming-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Rhoda Fleming opens with a bet that Mrs. Boulby's ears had not misheard. Robert would have fared badly that day without Mrs. Lovell's winning wager, Meredith notes. What seemed heroism to Warbeach appears in a different light, and the novel's ironies multiply.

The book's chapters glimpse what poor villainies the story contains, follow Edward taking his course, and introduce Major Percy Waring. Warbeach village church, a fearful temptation upon Anthony Hackbut, and his meeting with Dahlia follow. A study of a fool in trouble and Edward's letter close the book, as Rhoda's world darkens.
4429-evan-harrington-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens with the countess describing the field of action. Meredith pauses to clear up a point: readers may think the Comic Muse strains nature in making the countess rush open-eyed into danger. She has seen her brother pointed out as the tailor-fellow, yet she neither casts him off nor flies.

The book's chapters follow a capture, a small skirmish between Rose and Evan, and Evan writing himself tailor, then calling himself gentleman. The countess's campaign for rank meets Evan's honest love for Rose. This volume sharpens the novel's central joke: birth against breeding, and truth against show.
4437-vittoria-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Vittoria opens at the maestro's door, off the Borgo della Stella, where Carlo Ammiani conducts Vittoria to Rocco Ricci. They talk little on the way, and she asks him abruptly whether he is a good swordsman. He answers with the skill of perfect intimacy with the weapon, and she notes his father was a general.

The book's chapters follow Ammiani through the midnight, Countess Ammiani, and the Piazza d'Armi. The night of the fifteenth and the prima donna close the book. Vittoria's singing and the conspiracy draw together, as the revolution's night approaches and her voice becomes its signal.
4446-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Three of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens at a forest inn. Bowls of hot coffee and milk refresh Harry and Temple after a meal. White rolls to dip in them complete the fare. They talk like interchanging puffs of smoke, and the road soon brings a beautiful little lady accosting them in the forest.

The book's chapters promise the statue on the promontory. They promise the moment when Harry's father breathes, moves, and speaks. A delightful evening, a morning vision, and the return homeward follow. News of a fresh conquest of his father's, and a promenade in Bath, close the book. Harry's adventurer father steps fully into the story here.
4455-beauchamp-s-career-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career opens with Lord Palmet and certain electors, then a day at Itchincope and the question of examining the Whigs. A fine blow struck by Mr. Everard Romfrey follows, with the drive into Bevisham, Tourdestelle, and Beauchamp's holiday. The adventure of canvassing begins.

Nevil's radical candidacy meets the realities of an English borough: electors, landlords, newspapers, and family pressure. Meredith treats the election as comedy and as moral test. This volume shows Beauchamp learning that principle must survive contact with voters, rivals, and his own temper.
4463-the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-w:
Book Three of George Meredith's Tragic Comedians opens in a garden, where the heroine runs to the shade of the walls to read alone. Her own letter to the baroness crashes back sentence upon sentence, in retort, with the combative instinct of a beast. Twice she reads the lines with that defensive accompaniment, before they lay octopus limbs on her.

The baroness coldly states she has come to arrange matters, an answer that strikes chill as a glacier cave to a letter of fervid respect and supplication. This volume carries Lassalle's love story toward its fatal turn, as families, honor, and pride close in. Meredith's irony keeps the tragedy human, never merely grand.
4467-diana-of-the-crossways-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways opens with the authoress, as Diana turns her gifts to writing. A drive in sunlight and a drive in moonlight follow, with Diana's night-watch in the chamber of death. The young minister of state appears, and between Diana and Dacier the wind blows east over bleak land.

A visit from one of the world's good women follows, with a soul prepared for desperation, and once more the crossways and a change of turnings. A disappointed lover receives a multitude of lessons. This volume shows Diana at work and in danger, as authorship, politics, and love pull her toward scandal.
4473-one-of-our-conquerors-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's One of Our Conquerors opens on nature and circumstance, and the dissension between them, with a satirist's malignity toward his country. The great assembly at Lakeland follows, with Dartrey Fenellan and the intrusion of Jarniman. A lapdog named Tasso shows how minor causes produce momentous effects.

Nesta's engagement closes the book, as Victor Radnor's daughter steps toward marriage and independence. The conqueror's household, built on love outside the law, faces the world's judgment through his child. This volume mixes high comedy with the novel's moral pressure, as nature, society, and satire contend.
4479-lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta opens in a punctual household, where Mrs. Lawrence reports a cavalry messenger riding up the street. Weyburn directs a boy to ring the bell, and Lord Ormont goes to meet the day's business. The domestic opening hides the novel's military and marital maneuvers.

The book's chapters promise more of Cuper's boys, war at Olmer, and old lovers meeting new friends. A secret fished without angling follows, with two roads to Steignton. Ormont's past as a soldier and Aminta's present as his wife draw together, as brother, sister, and society press their claims.
4485-the-amazing-marriage-volume-3:
Book Three of George Meredith's Amazing Marriage opens with studies in fog, gout, an old seaman, a lovely serpent, and the moral effects of a borrowed shirt. Further glimpses of the wondrous mechanism of the younger man follow, with a right-minded great lady and Dame Gossip in her vein. A kidnapping with no great harm follows.

The philosopher man of action appears, with fencing, a descent into a steamer's engine room, and concessions to Mistress Gossip. Fleetwood's marriage to Carinthia, amazing in its mismatch, proceeds through comedy and crisis. This middle volume keeps Meredith's gossips busy, and his hero's pride under steady pressure.
4536-sylvia-s-lovers-volume-3:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers closes in this third volume, which runs from chapter thirty to chapter forty-five. Philip Hepburn, once poor and striving, now seems prosperous, with a flourishing business and money beyond his modest wants. Yet the chapter titles warn that ease will not last: happy days give way to evil omens, a rescue from the waves, an apparition, and a reckless recruit.

Later chapters bring mysterious tidings, bereavement, a recognition, confidences, an unexpected messenger, and a closing turn described as saved and lost. Readers who have followed Sylvia, Philip, and their rivals through the first two volumes will find the threads drawn together here. New readers should start earlier, since this volume assumes the loves, lies, and losses already in play.
4727-john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume:
Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr., closes his memoir of John Lothrop Motley in this third volume, opening in 1874, when Motley was sixty. Chapter twenty-two takes up the Life of John of Barneveld, with criticisms and Groen van Prinsterer. The full title of Motley's next and last work, Holmes notes, is The Life and Death of John of Barneveld, Advocate of Holland.

This volume therefore treats Motley as historian at the height of his powers, defending and explaining a Dutch statesman of an earlier age. It follows his later years, his writing, and his standing among critics, after the diplomatic and historical work of earlier volumes. Readers should start with volumes one and two, since this volume assumes Motley's life, friendships, and quarrels already known, and it brings his story to its close.
4773-the-letters-of-horace-walpole-earl-:
The Letters of Horace Walpole, Earl of Orford, including letters first published from original manuscripts, runs to four volumes, and this third volume covers 1759 to 1769. Its 1759 contents open with a letter to Montagu on November 17, on Temple's resignation of the privy seal and Lady Carlisle's marriage with Musgrave. A letter to Pitt on November 19 congratulates him on his administration's lustre.

A letter to Sir Horace Mann on November 30 reports Hawke's victory over Conflans and Kinnoul's mission to Portugal. A December 13 letter to Mann has Walpole regretting his ignorance of mathematics and common figures, and reporting Prince Henry's victory. December 23 brings a letter to Montagu on tumults in Ireland and a story of Lyttelton and Shelley, and one to Zouch on Clarendon and Lucan. The year 1760 opens with a visit to Emily and commotions in Ireland. Readers get Walpole's letters from a decade of war and politics.
4799-the-complete-poetical-works-of-perc:
The Complete Poetical Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley, volume three, is the Oxford edition of 1914, edited by Thomas Hutchinson. It includes materials never before printed, and this volume gathers Shelley's translations. Its contents open with a Hymn to Mercury, translated from Homer, followed by Homer's hymns to Castor and Pollux, the Moon, the Sun, the Earth, Minerva, and Venus.

The Cyclops, a satyric drama from Euripides, follows, with epigrams from Plato, including To Stella, Kissing Helena, and Circumstance. A fragment of the elegy on the death of Adonis, from the Greek of Bion, appears. A fragment of the elegy on the death of Bion, and Pan, Echo, and the Satyr, come from Moschus. Pieces from Vergil's tenth eclogue and fourth georgic, a sonnet from Dante, and the first canzone of the Convito close the contents. Readers get Shelley as translator of Greek, Latin, and Italian verse.
4911-wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-cons:
John Richardson's Wacousta continues in this third volume aboard a schooner where superstitious mariners fear their silent steersman. The crew, worn by anxiety, whispers that the steersman is a spirit sent to warn them of evil, and Fuller's repeated warnings through a sleepless night deepen their dread.

The volume carries the Pontiac conspiracy tale toward its close, with frontier sieges, disguised enemies, and personal revenge still driving the plot. Richardson keeps the lake and fort country vivid throughout. Readers who followed the first volumes get the payoff here: mystery resolved through action rather than explanation alone.
511-the-purcell-papers-volume-3:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu gathers Irish tales in this third volume of the Purcell Papers, framed as extracts from a parish priest's legacy. Jim Sulivan's adventures in the great snow open the book, with a Tyrone family history, a royalist captain's adventure, the Quare Gander, and Billy Malowney's taste of love and glory.

Le Fanu writes in rich Irish dialect, mixing humor, ghostly hints, and country talk. A memoir by Alfred Perceval Graves fronts the set. The volume preserves Le Fanu's early gift for Irish story, where a singer's luck, a wife's tongue, and a snowbound night can turn a life.
5236-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
Charles James Lever's Harry Lorrequer continues in this third volume, covering chapters eighteen through twenty-three. Harry takes up detachment duty in an assize town, spends a day in Dublin, passes a night at Howth. Harry journeys on toward Calais, with Fitzgerald's fear of prosecution for abduction hanging over the opening scenes.

The volume holds only this middle stretch of Harry's confessions, told in the same comic, anecdotal voice as the first. Readers following the novel in order will find assize courts, Irish towns. Cross-channel travel follows, all filtered through a young soldier's talent for getting into scrapes.
5463-the-sisters-volume-3:
A feast runs late in a vast peristyle in the third volume of Georg Ebers's The Sisters, as cups empty and carousers grow merrier and noisier. Elsewhere, a Roman and his friend Lysias walk up and down in their tent in violent agitation, speaking low. The contrast between revelry and worry drives the volume's opening.

The chapters move between banquet halls and private tents, where public celebration hides private plans. Ebers keeps Greek and Roman figures close together in Ptolemaic Egypt. Readers get a dramatic stretch of the romance, where a party's noise cannot drown out the trouble brewing beside it.
5469-joshua-volume-3:
Under a sycamore, only Miriam's low moans and a warrior's impatient footsteps break the quiet in the third volume of Georg Ebers's Joshua. The warrior struggles for composure and does not dare disturb her, unable to grasp what has risen like a mountain between him and the object of his love. He has learned from Hur that his father and Moses reject all mediation, yet he still bears promises.

The volume turns on love blocked by authority and divided loyalty among the Hebrews, with Moses and family elders standing firm. Ebers writes the personal conflict against the larger Exodus story. Readers get an emotional stretch of the romance, where private feeling meets unyielding leadership.
5799-life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-hu:
Volume three of the Life and Letters of Thomas Henry Huxley, edited by his son Leonard Huxley, covers the years 1887 through 1892 and beyond. Chapters run year by year, from 1887 through 1888, 1889, 1890 to 1891, and 1892, tracing Huxley's later career, controversies, and friendships. A portrait from a photograph by Downey in 1890 fronts the volume.

Readers meet the great Victorian biologist in his own words and in his circle's letters, debating evolution, agnosticism, and education. The volume shows Huxley as public champion of science and private correspondent, witty and combative by turns. It suits readers of Darwin's circle, Victorian science, and biography built from letters, offering the closing chapters of a formidable life.
