5810-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part three of Mark Twain's Following the Equator covers chapters twenty through twenty-nine, with a Pudd'nhead Wilson maxim on freedom of speech, freedom of conscience, and the prudence never to practice either. A diary note recalls Mr G, unseen since Nauheim in Germany several years earlier, when cholera broke out. From that reunion, the narrative moves through colonial towns and shipboard talk.

Twain gives his sharpest travel satire in compact form, as he weighs empire, race, and respectability against what he actually meets. The part favors anecdote and argument over scenery, letting a chance meeting open a wider reflection. It suits readers tracking Twain's world journey, and it offers some of the book's most quoted jokes about freedom and its limits.
5820-the-gilded-age-part-3:
Part three of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Warner, covers chapters nineteen through twenty-seven, and it opens with Harry Brierly drawing engineer's pay while living at the City Hotel in Hawkeye. Thompson kindly says it makes no difference whether Harry is with the corps or not. Harry still protests daily to the Colonel and to Washington Hawkins. He insists he must return at once to superintend the line. The gap between pay and work is the joke.

Readers follow Harry's easy life and the Hawkins family's schemes through Hawkeye and beyond, as railroads, land, and lobbying promise fortunes. The part favors comic character over plot machinery, letting Harry's charm carry scenes of delay and excuse. It suits readers midway through the novel, where satire of western enterprise grows sharper with every unpaid promise.
5838-sketches-new-and-old-part-3:
Part three of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old opens with Disgraceful Persecution of a Boy, a satire set in San Francisco. A well-dressed boy on his way to Sunday school, the sketch reports, was arrested and thrown into city prison for stoning Chinese men. Twain turns the incident into a commentary on human justice and our disposition to tyrannize the weak, with irony as his weapon.

Twain gives his moral satire at its most pointed, where a small news item exposes a large hypocrisy. The part gathers further sketches in first, second, and third sections, mixing comedy with protest. It suits readers who enjoy Twain as a critic of prejudice, and it shows how humor could carry a serious argument in his hands.
5856-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-vo:
Volume one, part three of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs covers chapters sixteen through twenty-four, at Chattanooga. Headings treat the enemy fortifying Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge, reorganizing the army, removing General Rosecrans, and punishing deserters. Grant arrives at Chattanooga, the fight on Lookout Mountain follows, a brave color bearer stands out, and the Battle of Missionary Ridge crowns the campaign.

It offers a general's account of a turning campaign, written with attention to positions, orders, and morale. Sheridan narrates from inside the army, praising courage and noting command changes without flinching. The part suits Civil War readers who want Chattanooga in a participant's voice, and it forms a key section of Sheridan's larger memoir of the war.
5862-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-:
Part three of Grant's Personal Memoirs covers chapters twenty-seven through thirty-eight, in the western campaigns. Headings move headquarters to Memphis, escape Jackson, handle complaints and requests, and note Halleck appointed commander in chief. A return to Corinth, movements of Bragg, surrender of Clarksville, advance upon Chattanooga, and Sheridan as colonel of a Michigan regiment follow.

Grant gives his account of command in the middle war, balancing logistics, politics, and battle with steady prose. The memoir explains decisions without boasting, letting orders, movements, and results carry the argument. It suits Civil War readers tracing Grant's rise, and it offers a clear, participant's view of the campaigns that shaped the western theater.
5902-journeys-through-bookland-vol-3:
Volume three of Sylvester's Journeys Through Bookland applies a new and original plan for reading to the world's best literature for children. Sylvester, author of English and American literature, presents the volume in a new edition, continuing the series' guided path through stories, poems, and classic tales. Each selection is chosen to lead a young reader onward, from simple delight to deeper reading.

Families get a structured anthology, where famous literature arrives in manageable pieces with context for parents and teachers. The volume favors breadth, mixing fancy, adventure, and moral tales without losing a child's attention. It suits homeschooling, bedtime reading, and anyone building a young reader's library, since the plan itself teaches how to love books.
5958-the-physiology-of-marriage-part-3:
Honoré de Balzac carries his study of marriage into open civil war between husband and wife. This third part offers meditations on manifestos and on the weapons science can put in a husband's hand. The husband stands single-handed, backed by religion and law, against a wife aided by native craft and social custom.

Balzac states his maxims bluntly, on love, deceit, and the erratic leaps by which women escape pursuit. He cares less for who will be vanquished than for whether resistance is possible at all. The tone is aphoristic and combative, treating wedlock as a contest with rules, allies, and beacons.
5968-what-s-mine-s-mine-volume-3:
George MacDonald opens the third volume with Mercy able to come down to the drawing room again. Evenings pass as never before, and quiet days give her time to think. She finds herself in a region of human life unlike any she has known, where every word and act seems to acknowledge something understood but unspoken.

The volume's chapters include a high school, a terrible discovery, love glooming, a generous dowry, the marches, midnight, the power of darkness, and a flitting to a new village. Alister and his princess figure late in the list.
6097-amelia-volume-3:
Henry Fielding's Amelia, volume three, opens its ninth book looking backwards, then forward, through conversations between Dr. Harrison and others and a dialogue between Booth and Amelia. A surprising accident, perhaps unmatched in history, and a scene of modern wit follow.

Two strangers appear, a curious conversation joins doctor, young clergyman, and the clergyman's father, and the tenth book presses on. Fielding brings Booth's prison past and Amelia's patience toward reckoning. What follows belongs strictly to the closing instalment, so the earlier instalments are not retraced or summarised here. Dr. Harrison's counsel steadies Booth through the final trials.
6176-pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-:
Shon McGann's Tobogan Ride opens Parker's third volume. Shon lies on buffalo robes in a mountain hut, singing of Farcalladen Rise with knees pressed to saddle, sparks from hoofs, and hearts beating hard toward the glen. He vows never to go back to Farcalladen more.

Pretty Pierre, Jo Gordineer, the Honourable Just Trafford, and Prince Levis share the hut, pipe smoke, and song. Pere Champagne, The Scarlet Hunter, and The Stone complete the volume. Attention here rests only on the third set of tales, not on any tale belonging to another set. Song and snow carry the volume's tales along.
6188-northern-lights-volume-3:
When the Swallows Homeward Fly opens Parker's third Northern Lights volume, as an arrogant sun stalks into evening trailing gold and crimson banners, and swift twilight streams over land. Two men on a high hill watch it pass, one with a look like light in a window to a lost traveler.

That man made a journey few attempted and fewer finished, traveling on foot and alone, save dogs and Indian guides, to snowy Arctic regions where a continent's shoulder juts into northwestern seas. Ice hummocks housed him, pemmican and raw fish fed him. George's Wife and Marcile complete the volume.
6208-the-trail-of-the-sword-volume-3:
The third part of The Trail of the Sword begins with a chapter whose title turns water into wine. Three months on, George Gering looks ahead with delight to a pair of sea journeys. His appetite for one journey sharpens his appetite for the other, although treasure hunting pleases most men no more than a wedding does.

Gering already carries Jessica's promise to marry him, and he soon departs beside William Phips toward Spanish territory. When he reaches New York again, word that Hudson's Bay posts have fallen spreads alarm through the town. Colonel Richard Nicholls grows furious at the news, while Jessica, staying at Government House, feels deeply shaken.
6213-the-translation-of-a-savage-volume-:
The Faith of Comrades opens the third volume of The Translation of a Savage. Francis Armour steps out of his wife's room, goes downstairs without noise to the library, and takes a seat there. Nothing feels lonelier, he reflects, than facing his own conscience alone.

An enemy can hand a man a harsh hour, a friend can hand him a grieving hour, and time by himself can hand him a quiet hour. Yet when conscience settles upon each small rise of memory and gestures slowly, a labourer driven around a treadmill suffers no greater pain. The butler comes in to learn what is wanted, and Armour dismisses him with a silent wave.
6221-the-trespasser-volume-3:
Gaston Belward spends his mornings in the family solicitor's office, turning over old papers with a strange sense that something waits to be found. A clerk brings him a small box found inside another box of the Belward-Staplings, a distant branch of the family, and the key still sits in its lock. The find opens the last part of his story, where past deeds press hard on present choices.

These closing chapters carry Belward afar, set him between two worlds, and bring the old Adam of his nature face to face with love. A woman and a man confront what they cannot bear, and an old biblical call sounds over the end. Parker closes his romance of claim and heritage with passion, guilt, and a plea for return.
6226-the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-3:
Moray has been shut from the outer world for months, with a new jailer in place of Gabord and sentinels who refuse all news. He hears nothing of Alixe, little of Doltaire or Bigot, and no sign at all of Voban. The chapters here take him through a chamber of torture and past the bars of his cage. Then comes a steep path of conquest, with a dancer and the Bastille waiting in his tale.

This middle volume is the prison book of Parker's memoir, tense with waiting, watching, and small acts of will. Moray studies his jailer as closely as his jailer studies him, and every scrap of news becomes precious. It shows a captive officer keeping his mind sharp while his fate is argued by powers far beyond his cell walls.
6232-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
The night and morning after Guida's marriage pass slowly, and the day wears on toward the sailing of the Narcissus. Guida works at home with feverish unrest, settles her grandfather in his great armchair for his afternoon sleep, and spins and sings as he drowses. From her kitchen door she can see blue water, a perfect sky, and Noirmont Point, round which her husband's ship will soon vanish.

This middle volume follows a new wife left behind while a ship puts to sea, with neighbours watching and tongues ready to judge. Maitresse Aimable fingers her rosary for Guida, and the island's small world presses close. Parker writes the parting in domestic detail, so that a single afternoon of spinning, waiting, and watching carries the weight of a marriage just made.
6239-the-lane-that-had-no-turning-volume:
Annette has kept her dot ready for many months, chest, bed, linen, and yarn inventoried each day, first with pride and then more shyly, as Benoit does not come. He promised to return with the first drive of logs in summer, when the little church of St. Saviour's would bless their marriage. Benoit has the brightest scarf, the merriest laugh, and the quickest eyes in Pontiac, and almost anyone would have believed him.

This volume gathers eight Pontiac tales around Annette's wait and a miller's marriage. Mathurin, a lime-burner, a woodsman's story of a great white chief, Uncle Jim, a house with a tall porch, and Parpon the dwarf complete the set. Parker writes village courtship and work with affection and irony, letting a delayed lover stand for all the hopes a parish pins on one summer. The comedy is gentle, the ache beneath it real.
6252-michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-sword:
Leicester, a man of high place whose hand has tied and untied knots of court intrigue for years, stoops in this volume to a small game that earns him scorn. He has turned the Queen's mind and foiled Spanish, German, and French diplomacy. He checkmated the Medici by hidden means, yet he stands hated by most and loved by none save a royal mistress who now keeps him more from custom than affection. His rise, built on labour and rashness alike, begins to cost him.

This third volume sets a young woman against the Earl, as she refuses to measure swords with him and yet will not yield. She tells him plainly that she has friends, and that in her greatest need she will go seeking them, thinking of the Queen. Parker writes court power as a trap, where the grandest player can look smallest when he bullies the unfriended.
6258-donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-eg:
Wyndham Bimbashi's career in Egypt has been a run of mistakes, Parker begins, for he is opinionated, unlucky, and fond of grave acts on his own light responsibility. He scorns the native mind and the native official, and lacks the gift his fellow countrymen often show of working through local custom toward sound rule. High-handed acts of his cause riots in native villages, and the man at the wheel must answer for the course he steers.

This third volume pairs that tale with a tyrant and a lady. A woman by the Nile writes steadily for an hour, then looks up at muddy water, laden boats, and Muslims at prayer with faces toward Mecca. Parker sets British bluster beside Egyptian patience, and lets both meet on the river. The two stories show power misused and power endured, where one officer's temper can shake a district.
6270-embers-volume-3:
Camden Town opens this volume in verse, asking how many years of sun and snow have passed since the poet wandered its streets and shade. Days turn out to be years, and years forever, while joys and ills press on heart and brain as the only true measures of age. The poet, young in years, feels old in all these, and wonders if he knows the man his younger self begot.

This third volume of poems runs from Camden Town through Juniper Cove and its twenty years after, listening, nevertheless, Ishmael, and over the hills. A deliverer, a desert road, a son of the Nile, a farewell from the harem, and an Arab love song follow, with a camel driver, a tall Daboon, and Nell Latore. Parker writes travel and memory in short lines, where a place name alone can open a whole past.
6277-the-money-master-volume-3:
A young singer at the Manor Cartier asks who will walk the wood with her, for she fears to walk alone and has known no dangers. Applause breaks out at the last note, with cries of encore, and she looks round with frank pleasure on the little group about her. A particular person answers, the Man from Outside, sitting near a bright wood fire on a cool night near June, delicate and fluent in French with a slight English accent.

This third epoch holds only three chapters: the man from outside, a refusal to go, and a good market. The singer is asked for a perfect song, a clear fountain tune ringing in her head all day, while toasts rise to Jean Jacques Barbille. Parker writes a brief, bright interval, where music and company soften a life that has known harder dealing, before misfortune gathers again.
6283-the-world-for-sale-volume-3:
It is a fine day, Fleda says, and Ingolby, blind, agrees, though she wonders from delicacy how he knows. He explains with a dreamy smile, hands smoothing a coverlet like a wrinkled map, that the blind gain new senses. A light breath of wind, fresh crisp air, the smell of sun, a light frost showing dry ground, and wild fowl crying south all tell him. One sense less gives more power to the rest.

This final book runs from two life pieces and a fowler's snare through a secret man. The return of Belisarius, at long last, man proposes, a sleeper, and the world for sale follow. Fleda watches a primeval scene and dreams of sight restored, with a hovering sense of invasion at its edge. Parker closes his western tale with patience, as love learns to see without eyes.
6294-no-defense-volume-3:
A planter sighs at his writing table on Christmas Day and looks out over lands he made his own on the Thomas River, hours from Spanish Town. Plateau, mountains, and ravines frame the estate. He has done his duty to slaves and folk, with presents, a morning breakfast, and festivities. A feast in Creole style follows for attorneys, overseers, and officers. He turns with cynicism from an overladen table centred on stewed wild boar.

This third book brings a letter, strangers, Salem, and Lord Mallow intervening, with a clash of race and Sheila having her say. The coming of Noreen and a visit with the governor follow, and the question of what happened next hangs over all. Parker moves his Irish tale to Jamaica, where a planter's Christmas plenty cannot hide old wounds, and Dyck Calhoun, seen at Spanish Town, carries prison's mark into a new world.
6298-carnac-s-folly-volume-3:
Months pass, and destiny makes new drawings, Parker says, as Carnac goes with his mother to paint at Charlemont. Tarboe works the mills with success. Junia hears from Carnac in a letter that reads like a friend's yet carries sadness. Then she leaves west again at an hour's notice to nurse her aunt. Quebec politics boil as the Dominion government nears the polls, and even secluded cottages on the St. Lawrence argue the administration's virtues and faults.

This third book moves from a great decision to Carnac as candidate, news heard by Junia and Tarboe, a secret meeting, and point to point contests. A man who would not, a blue paper, a challenge, and an exit follow, with a woman's letter and a dream by Tarboe. Parker closes the tale with politics, painting, and a way home found at last.
6441-uncle-robert-s-geography-uncle-robe:
Francis W. Parker and Nellie Lathrop Helm, in the Home Reading Series, send Uncle Robert to visit a farm family, where children's knowledge of farm life is warmly recognised. Children feel his sympathy for their work and are led to closer study, for everything they see and do matters, exalting daily life. Descriptions of farms should cover plant and animal life and the means and processes of farm work.

Frank draws a map of the farm, and drawing, modelling, and painting enter early, for children draw boldly unless criticism outruns skill. A new thermometer, animals, flower garden, sunlight and shadow, and a barometer follow, with a walk in the woods, birds and flowers, and a thundershower. Susie plants mignonette seeds in soft, warm soil and asks if they will grow. Parker writes geography as farm life, learned by doing.
6457-the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-a:
Frances Burney's diary and letters, volume three, covers 1792 to 1840, with notes by W. C. Ward and Lord Macaulay's essay as preface. The volume opens with French political emigrants at Juniper Hall and Miss Burney's marriage to M. d'Arblay. Arrivals, the Doctor's five daughters, a visit to Arthur Young, and the Duke de Liancourt's abortive efforts at Rouen and escape to England fill the early pages.

Madame de Genlis's hasty retreat, a nobleman of the ancien regime, ducal vivacity and sadness, and graceful offers of hospitality follow, with severe decrees against emigrants and revolutionary societies in the background. A mid letter turns indignant at a man whose first prepossession the writers conquered by pains, only to see him act as coadjutor with Barras and other villains. Burney writes revolution as lived experience, in letters and diary entries close to events.
7135-the-great-conspiracy-volume-3:
Logan's third part of The Great Conspiracy opens at chapter eleven, The Causes of Secession. It recalls that from the Republic's birth some citizens hated it, and when they could not rule, worked by conspiracy, sedition, mutiny, nullification, secession, or otherwise to weaken and destroy it. Edward McPherson's documentary History of the Rebellion states the process well, Logan says, noting a considerable body in slaveholding states always disaffected to the Union.

They resisted the Constitution's adoption, then sought to refine away the general government's rights and powers. By artful expedients over years, using excitements from passing questions, they finally perverted public sentiment. Only this third part's argument is traced here, as Logan builds the case that secession was no sudden passion but a long conspiracy.
7152-cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-vo:
Burney's Cecilia reaches its third volume at book eight, continued, with a chapter titled An Event. Cecilia, scarce less unhappy in her decision than in her uncertainty, sits dissatisfied with her situation, her views, and herself, still distressed and uncomfortable when Delvile calls the next morning. He cannot discover what her determination has been, and fearfully asks his doom with hardly any hope of favor.

Cecilia, above affectation and a stranger to art, refuses to keep him an instant in suspense, since she herself is no longer in suspense. She owns she may have seemed trifling, but insists she has been nothing less, and that Delvile would excuse her of caprice if he knew half the distress of her irresolution. Only this third volume's course is followed here, toward the heiress's hard won resolution.
7156-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-3:
Part three of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter eight, The Question of the Seal, with Henry the Eighth waking about five o'clock from an unrefreshing nap. Troublous dreams, he mutters, and his end now at hand, as warnings and failing pulses confirm it. Yet a wicked light flames in his eye as he vows he will not die till he go before, meaning the man whose doom waits.

Attendants find him awake and ask his pleasure on the Lord Chancellor waiting without, and the king cries admit him eagerly. The chancellor kneels by the couch reporting that peers in robes stand at the bar, having confirmed the Duke of Norfolk's doom, and humbly await further pleasure. The king's face lights with fierce joy, crying lift me up, for in his own person he will go before his parliament.
7195-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-3:
Part Three of Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer finds Tom dodging through lanes to shake off returning scholars, then falling into a moody jog toward Cardiff Hill. He crosses a small branch two or three times, trusting a juvenile superstition that crossing water baffles pursuit, and at last he slips behind the Douglas mansion into a dense wood.

Under a spreading oak, in dead noonday heat that has stilled even the birds, Tom sits on a mossy spot to brood alone. The scene shows the boy at his most romantic and solitary, turning a walk into a small epic of escape. This part holds the woodland mood and Tom's lonely wanderings, before the tale turns back to village trouble.
7244-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Three opens in slow torture on a lovely autumn morning. The Yankee and his company ride through sylvan solitudes in the first freshness of the day. Fair green valleys spread below hilltops, streams wind through them, island groves and huge lonely oaks cast black blots of shade, and distant castles fleck the hazy hills.

Broad lawns sparkling with dew carry the riders onward, and Twain lets the beauty of the land sit oddly beside the chapter's grim title. The Yankee's modern eye notes both the landscape and the hard customs waiting beyond it. This part holds the country ride and its mix of charm and menace, before the plot tightens again.
733-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon carried his history through the reign of Theodosius in this third volume, with notes by H. H. Milman. It covers the death of Gratian, the ruin of Arianism, the civil wars against Maximus and Eugenius, and the penance and death of Theodosius himself. St. Ambrose and the court at Milan play large parts.

The volume then turns to the final destruction of pagan worship and the rise of saints and relics among Christians, and to the division of the empire between the sons of Theodosius. Gibbon's narrative stays stately and sharp, weighing emperors, bishops, and generals alike. It is a key stretch of the story, where one empire becomes two.
7533-a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-3:
The third volume of Beverley Nichols's old ballads opens with Clerk Colvill and his lusty dame walking in the garden. It runs through some of the darkest and finest of the old songs. Sir Aldingar, Edom o' Gordon, and Chevy Chace follow, with Sir Lancelot du Lake, Gil Morrice, and the Child of Elle. Child Waters and King Edward IV and the Tanner of Tamworth add love and disguise.

Sir Patrick Spens, the shipwreck ballad, closes the main sequence before the Earl of Mar's Daughter, and color plates picture Clerk Colvill, Gil Morrice, Child Waters, and the Earl's daughter. Nichols's selection favors narrative force over prettiness: betrayal, murder, and loyalty told in stark verse. The volume is a strong draught of the ballad tradition at its most dramatic.
7752-godolphin-volume-3:
Constance, Countess of Erpingham, sits alone as a young bride in the third volume of Lytton's Godolphin, in a splendid room full of flowers and scent. Below, the old Mall in June crowds with riders and walkers, yet her brow has lost its glad pride, as if the gift she wanted also pierced her heart.

Her husband asks if she will ride today, while talk turns to diplomacy, assemblies, and her conquest over Lady Delville. Through a bride's lonely hours, the volume shows how rank and wealth can leave a woman alone in a city that worships both.
7759-falkland-book-3:
Lady Emily Mandeville's journal fills Book Three of Lytton's Falkland, in dated entries of joy and guilt. Julia arrives kind and silent, and Emily weeps in her arms without words, a confession and repentance both. No letter comes for days, then a note: he has returned, and she is wild with fear.

Sunday brings the meeting she cannot resist, though she knows his reasons are sophistry and his spell blocks escape. A dinner and ball follow, with Falkland among the guests. The journal form lays bare a woman's heart day by day, between longing, shame, and a love she cannot master.
8168-gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrate:
Book three of Rabelais's Gargantua and Pantagruel turns from war to a question: should Panurge marry? Panurge seeks counsel everywhere, from theologians, lawyers, doctors, and philosophers, and each answer deepens his doubt. Urquhart's translation of this book appeared posthumously in 1693, with a new edition of books one and two under Motteux's editorship. And the text here draws on those editions, with passages restored from the 1738 edition edited by Ozell.

The third book is Rabelais's most discursive, a comic symposium on marriage, fate, and free will that ends with a decision to consult the Oracle of the Holy Bottle. Its learned jokes and lists remain famous. For readers following Pantagruel's company, this is the philosophical heart of the sequence, and its funniest debate.
8463-memoirs-of-henry-hunt-esq-volume-3:
Volume 3 of Henry Hunt's memoirs continues the radical orator's story, written by himself in His Majesty's jail at Ilchester, in Somerset. Hunt, jailed in the Peterloo era, uses the volume to defend his career, attack his enemies, and argue for parliamentary reform, with Pope's lines on faultless pieces again as epigraph.

Readers meet early nineteenth-century radical politics from inside, as Hunt tells it: crowds, trials, and the press wars that made him famous and hated. The memoirs are vivid and one-sided, which is their value as history. Together with volumes 1 and 2, they form a prison-written account of a movement.
8473-life-on-the-mississippi-part-3:
Part 3 of Life on the Mississippi drops readers into chapter 11, The River Rises, where a big rise turns small craft into a nuisance. Twain's boat runs chute after chute, a new world to the young pilot. Broad-horns, flatboats, appear in the worst places: cramped bends, and the head of a chute, where a collision seems certain.

This section shows Twain learning the river's dangers in high water, with humor and close observation of boats, crews, and currents. Readers get the pilot's education in mid-course, after the geography of part 1 and the cub-pilot chapters. It is river life at its most crowded and comic, with the Mississippi itself as the chief character.
8513-the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-vo:
Volume 3 of Émile Zola's Lourdes, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, covers the third day of the pilgrimage. At seven on a fine August Sunday morning, Guersaint is already up and dressed. He secured one of two little rooms on the third floor of the Hotel of the Apparitions, and now he goes to begin the day's devotions.

Zola follows the pilgrims through the third day's processions, hopes, and disappointments, with Pierre and Marie at the center. The volume shows Lourdes as a small city of faith and commerce, where miracles are sought and counted. Readers following the trilogy get the pilgrimage at its height, in Zola's detailed, naturalist manner.
8528-eve-s-diary-part-3:
Adam's voice takes over in Part 3 of Mark Twain's Eve's Diary, and his gruff tone softens into fond observation. He reminds himself to allow for Eve's youth, since she is still only a girl. Everything strikes her as wonderful, and a fresh flower stops her with delight, prompting her to pet and caress it.

This section gives Adam's gruff, fond view of Eve, after her own diary entries in earlier parts. Readers get Twain's comic marriage, told from both sides, with Adam learning to love wonder itself. The part suits readers who know the whole diary, and those who want Adam's voice alone.
8553-the-seaboard-parish-volume-3:
George MacDonald closes The Seaboard Parish in volume 3. Its contents include A Walk with My Wife, Our Last Shore-Dinner, A Pastoral Visit, and The Art of Nature. The Sore Spot, The Gathering Storm, The Gathered Storm, The Shipwreck, The Funeral, The Sermon, Changed Plans, and The Studio follow.

The final volume brings the parish story to storm and loss, with a shipwreck and a funeral testing the minister's faith and his people. MacDonald's seaside parish, with its sermons and family life, ends in reflection on nature, art, and grief. Readers following the trilogy get its resolution, gentle and earnest, by the sea that shaped it.
8584-roughing-it-part-3:
This third part of Mark Twain's Roughing It picks up at chapter twenty-one, as the stagecoach nears Carson City, capital of Nevada Territory, on the twentieth day of the journey. Twain and his companions are sorry to stop: they have grown fond of stage life, fed on wonders daily, and now face a humdrum village walled in by barren, snow-clad mountains. Sagebrush, greasewood, and alkali dust replace the road's variety.

From Carson City the narrative turns to Nevada settlement, mining hopes, and the daily grind of a raw frontier town. The comedy sharpens as Twain's grand plans meet dust, disappointment, and small-time scheming. Readers who enjoyed the overland journey will find the same voice now applied to staying put, and the same mix of tall tale and sharp observation that made the book endure.
8595-normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its:
Mont St Michel opens this third part of Gordon Home's illustrated tour of Normandy, first seen from the coast road out of Avranches. Home describes the long approach across sands and causeway, the walled rock rising from the bay, and the small villages, wells, and farmyards passed on the way. Sunset light, grey seas, and the tide flooding the road all shape how the mount first appears.

After the mount, the tour moves on to Coutances and the Cotentin coast, then St Lo, Bayeux, Caen, and the shore toward Trouville, ending with notes on Norman history. The chapters blend road notes, building detail, and old stories, so a reader can follow the same ground Home walked. It works best as a companion for anyone planning to visit, or simply picturing, these towns.
8703-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-3:
This third volume of Gustave Dore's Bible gallery moves from judges to kings, opening with Deborah's song of triumph after Israel's victory. Deborah and Barak sing praise for a people who offered themselves willingly, recalling the Lord marching out of Seir and Edom while earth trembled and mountains melted. Jephthah met by his daughter, and Jephthah's daughter with her companions, follow, with Samson slaying the lion, Samson and Delilah, and the death of Samson.

Naomi and her daughters-in-law, Ruth and Boaz, the return of the ark, and Saul and David, with David sparing Saul, complete the volume's arc from tribal judges to the monarchy's beginnings. The passages, chosen to match Dore's engravings, favour dramatic turning points. Readers meet some of the Old Testament's most retold stories in compact form, and can trace how Israel's leaders rose, fell, and passed power onward.
8723-the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volum:
This third volume of Emile Zola's Rome, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, is Part III of the novel, opening with Pierre, after a long ramble, once more before the Vatican. A harassing attraction ever leads him there. On a Wednesday evening he meets Monsignor Nani, assessor of the Holy Office, fresh from his weekly audience with the Pope, where he reported the Congregation's morning proceedings. Nani, smiling with pleasant civility, offers Pierre a chance to see the Pope in public while waiting for a private audience.

From that meeting, the volume follows Pierre deeper into Vatican circles, where politeness masks surveillance and delay. Zola contrasts Pierre's earnest hope for a hearing with a system skilled at wearing petitioners down. The middle volume tightens the novel's suspense: will Pierre ever reach the Pope, and what will Rome do with a priest who wants the Church to change?
8792-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
This third part of Cary's Purgatory covers cantos eleven through eighteen, the terraces of pride, envy, and wrath. Canto eleven opens with a paraphrase of the Lord's Prayer, addressed to the Almighty Father who makes the heavens his dwelling, not confined by bounds. Viewing his primal effluence with intenser love there. The proud, bent under stones, join their voices to the prayer for daily manna, for peace, and for forgiveness.

Envious souls with sewn eyes, wrathful souls in blinding smoke. Virgil's great discourse on love and free will follow, as Dante learns why disordered love is the root of sin. The part is Purgatory's teaching heart, moving from punishment to philosophy without losing poetry. Readers who want Dante's moral theory in its clearest form will find it here, carried by prayer, example, and Virgil's patient argument on the mountain road.
8798-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Cary's Paradise concludes in this third part, cantos twenty-two through thirty-three, the highest heavens. Canto twenty-two turns, astounded, to Beatrice as guardian of his steps, like a child running to where he trusts most. She soothes him like a mother calming a pale, breathless son. She reminds him that he is in Heaven, where all is holy and all is done zealously and well. Asks what change her song and smile have wrought in him.

From the contemplatives' heaven, Dante rises through the fixed stars, the primum mobile, and the Empyrean, to the rose of the blessed and the final vision of God. The part's last cantos, with Bernard as guide, are among the most famous in literature. Readers finishing the Comedy here meet Dante's attempt to say the unsayable.
884-memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-del:
Charles Mackay devoted this third volume to three more delusions: alchemy, fortune telling, and animal magnetism. The alchemists, searchers for the philosopher's stone and the water of life, run from Geber and Avicenna through Albertus Magnus, Roger Bacon, Nicholas Flamel, and Paracelsus to Cagliostro and St. Germain.

Fortune tellers and magnetisers follow, with their dupes and their arts, and Mackay notes that dissatisfaction with one's lot drives much human folly, yet also much progress. His moral is clear: reason must guard against wonder. The volume completes his classic survey of crowd madness, and it still reads as a warning.
892-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
This third volume follows Rome through civil war and the reign of Theodosius, the emperor who tried to hold a splitting empire together. Gratian dies, Arianism falls, and Theodosius fights Maximus and Eugenius, wins, does penance under St. Ambrose, and dies, leaving the empire to his sons.

Gibbon then traces the end of pagan worship, the rise of saints and relics, and the final division of East and West. Milman's notes accompany the text. The volume marks the hinge of the whole history, where one Roman world becomes two, and where faith begins to shape the state as much as armies do.
8943-adela-cathcart-volume-3:
George MacDonald wrote Adela Cathcart as a frame tale: a sick young woman is cheered by stories told aloud by family and friends. This third volume carries on the frame with Uncle Peter, and adds tales such as The Giant's Heart, The Cruel Painter, and The Castle. Each story is meant to lift Adela's spirits and stir her mind.

MacDonald's tales blend fairy wonder with moral depth, and the talks between stories let his characters weigh what each tale means. The book shows his gift for using fantasy to heal and teach. Readers who love Victorian fairy tales will find this volume warm, strange, and full of heart.
8956-the-literary-remains-of-samuel-tayl:
Henry Nelson Coleridge collects and edits the third volume of Samuel Taylor Coleridge's literary remains, published in 1838 and inscribed to John Hookham Frere. Contents open with a letter to a godchild from Lincoln's Inn, March 26, 1838, followed by a Formula Fidei on the Holy Trinity from 1830. One piece presents the absolute as pure subjectivity, good by its very nature, and as the ground and will behind all possible being.

Later remains range through theology, philosophy, and literary criticism, in fragments, notes, and letters that show Coleridge's mind working after his poetic prime. Henry Nelson Coleridge, the poet's nephew and son-in-law, preserves material that might otherwise have vanished. Scholars of Romanticism value the volume for Coleridge's late thought. General readers will find demanding but rewarding glimpses of a mind that never stopped theologizing, even in private notes.
9166-the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volu:
Émile Zola wrote Paris as the third book of his Three Cities trilogy, translated by Ernest Vizetelly. This volume holds Book Three, called The Rivals. On the Wednesday before mid-Lent Thursday, a great charity bazaar fills the Duvillard mansion for the Asylum of the Invalids of Labour. Five thousand cards admit all Paris society.

The opening of the bombarded mansion to crowds is an event, watched by police in nearby streets. Duvillard planned the bazaar, and his wife obeyed his bidding. Zola uses the glitter to expose wealth, power, and charity as show. The volume drives the trilogy toward crisis.
9317-a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-3:
Ian Maclaren's Book Three, A Fight with Death, centers on Saunders, Drumsheugh's grieve, brought to death's gates by fever caught in Glasgow. A London doctor at Lord Kilspindie's lodge looks in from the moor and gives him six hours, more or less. He buttons his gloves, climbs into his brake, and leaves the verdict behind.

Bell hears it from behind the door and gives way utterly, but Drumsheugh will not accept it while Saunders still lives. Dr. MacLure's fight for the man follows, quiet and stubborn. The volume is Maclaren at his most moving, a parable of hope against medical pride.
9445-samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-:
Part three of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren picks up Samantha's church and home battles in mid-stream. Told in Holley's broad farm dialect, it follows Samantha and her husband Josiah through meeting-house strife and neighborly trials. This part opens as Josiah's temper shifts, and a silver wedding invite stirs the house. The tone stays comic, but the stakes feel real.

Lodema's sharp tongue, fair work, and church funds tangle through the chapters, with Samantha striving to keep peace and win a hearing for women. Josiah, slow to change, gives ground in small, telling ways. A reader gets more of Holley's beloved farm wife: jokes, grit, and a steady push for justice inside the church walls.
948-ethics-part-3:
Baruch Spinoza's Ethics continues in Part Three, on the origin and nature of the emotions, translated by R. H. M. Elwes. Spinoza notes that most writers on the emotions treat them as matters outside nature, rather than as natural phenomena following nature's general laws. He sets out to correct that error.

He defines joy, sorrow, desire, love, and hate as states of mind and body, following from causes as surely as any motion. His geometric order stays strict, and his aim is practical: to know the emotions is the first step to mastering them. Part Three is the heart of Spinoza's psychology, and it still rewards close reading.
9752-night-and-morning-volume-3:
Volume three of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning opens in a Paris quarter, before a curious temple-like building. Pilasters painted green and gilt, a semicircular front, and an entresol mark the odd house, which local virtuosi took for a Roman temple copy. The novel's plot thickens around this Paris scene, as fortunes and schemes cross. Lytton's eye for streets and rooms stays sharp.

Book three carries the tale through Paris society, art, and intrigue, with the temple house as its emblem. The prose favors polished scene painting. A reader gets the middle book of a Victorian novel of ambition, set in a Paris both fashionable and strange.
9881-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-:
Samuel Richardson's great epistolary novel tells its story entirely through letters, and this third volume carries Clarissa Harlowe's ordeal forward. Her friend Miss Howe urges her to marry Lovelace, while Clarissa recounts, in alarm, how Lovelace tricked her away from her family.

Letter by letter, readers watch Clarissa weigh duty, love, and fear, blaming her first secret letters to Lovelace for all that followed. Richardson's slow, inward method makes her mind the scene of the drama. This volume is essential for anyone following one of the longest and most famous novels in English.
a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-3:
Volume 3 of Beverley Nichols's A Book of Old Ballads draws again on Percy's Reliques and the English and Scottish ballads gathered by Child and Kittredge. It opens with 'Clerk Colvill,' warned by his wife never to ride by the wells of Slane, and riding there anyway to meet the mermaid who is his death.

Border and battle pieces dominate the middle of the volume: 'Edom o' Gordon,' the great hunting fight of 'Chevy Chace,' and 'Sir Patrick Spens' sailing to his drowning. 'Sir Lancelot du Lake,' 'Gil Morrice,' 'Child Waters,' and 'King Edward IV and the Tanner of Tamworth' mix romance, murder, and comedy, and 'The Earl of Mar's Daughter' closes the set. Four ballads carry colour plates.
a-collection-of-old-english-plays-volume: In the third volume of his old English plays, Arthur Henry Bullen prints one play for the first time. The other plays in the volume had likewise not been reprinted before. Bullen notes that a promised Heywood play defeated him, its handwriting being too hard to read. He hoped an expert in old handwriting might yet secure it for a later volume.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Part 3 sends Hank riding with Sandy through lovely country that turns to slow torture behind her endless tale-telling and armour he cannot scratch himself in. Their road passes freemen ground down by lords and Church, and Sandy narrates her own story of a castle, ogres, and swineherds in the approved romance style, at approved romance length.

The journey ends at the castle of Morgan le Fay, Arthur's sister, a queen beautiful, musical, and casually murderous with her prisoners and servants. Hank must manage her whims, her dungeons, and her terror of her guest's reputation as a magician. The part mixes travel writing, dialect comedy, and a hard account of what common people owed their betters in Twain's sixth century.
a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-3: The third volume of Ian Maclaren's Doctor of the Old School follows Saunders to the gates of death by fever. A London doctor at a shooting lodge gives him six hours and leaves in his carriage. Bell hears the verdict from behind the door and gives way to grief. The volume tests the parish doctor against a famous oracle from the city.
a-far-country-volume-3:
Winston Churchill opens book three of his novel with the fame of Hugh Paret's city. It is a byword for sudden, fabulous wealth. It turns out a full-fledged millionaire, so it was said, nearly every week. Distinguished Englishmen, Frenchmen, Germans, and Italians on the grand tour made a point of visiting, and exhausted their adjectives on the place.

This final volume brings Paret's climb to its reckoning. The corporation lawyer who mastered the city's machinery faces the emptiness of the life he built, the marriage it starved, and the claims of a conscience he outran for years. Churchill closes his panoramic novel of American business with judgment and a hard-won turn toward honesty.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-3:
William Dean Howells opens the third part of his New York novel with a banquet swelling in the promoter Fulkerson's fancy. The magazine Every Other Week has succeeded, and Fulkerson dreams of a dinner at Delmonico's with the literary and artistic people of the whole country, fully reported in the papers. His genius is for turning literature into an event.

Around the scheme the novel's strands tighten: old Dryfoos's pride in his money's new respectability, his son Conrad's feeling for the poor, and the artists' and writers' jostling for place. Howells keeps his large cast in motion with talk as the main action. The volume carries the magazine from experiment to institution, with the costs showing.
a-history-of-science-volume-3:
Henry Smith Williams devotes the third volume of his history to the modern development of the physical sciences. The contents begin with Newton's successors in astronomy, Halley, Bradley, Herschel, and Laplace among them, and the slow solution of the shape of the earth. New fields then open one after another.

Chapters cover the birth of paleontology, modern geology, and meteorology, then heat, light, electricity, and magnetism. The conservation of energy and the ether get chapters of their own. Williams, helped by Edward H. Williams, writes plainly for lay readers and keeps the human story of each discoverer in view. The volume carries science from the telescope age into the laboratory age.
a-life-for-a-life-volume-1-of-3:
Volume one of A Life for a Life, an 1859 novel by Dinah Maria Mulock Craik, opens a story issued in the three-volume form Victorian readers expected. Craik was a popular novelist of domestic life, best known for John Halifax, Gentleman. This first volume begins the tale that the following two volumes carry to its close.

As the opening installment, it sets out the characters and the stakes implied by the title, in which a life answers for a life. Craik's fiction is known for its earnest moral feeling and its close attention to home and work. Readers who finish this volume hold the first act of the full novel, in the same divided form in which its first audience read it.
a-popular-history-of-france-from-the-ear: François Guizot continues his history of France through the later Hundred Years' War. It runs from Charles the Sixth and the dukes of Burgundy to Charles the Seventh and Joan of Arc. The volume then follows Louis the Eleventh and the wars in Italy under Charles the Eighth and Louis the Twelfth. Illustrations of Joan entering Orleans, Chinon Castle, and the States General at Tours mark the passage from civil strife to a kingdom taking firmer shape.
a-romance-of-youth-volume-3:
Francois Coppee carries his hero into later boyhood in A Romance of Youth, Volume 3 of the English edition. Amedee now studies and dreams beyond the Gerard family's rooms. The engraver's daughters are growing into young women beside him. Childhood's pretend marriage starts to cast a real shadow over all three hearts.

Paris widens for Amedee in this volume: schools, streets, and first ambitions enter the tale. Money stays scarce, and pride becomes a young man's defense. Coppee follows the shift from games to glances with a poet's patience for detail. Family sorrows and neighbors' kindnesses still steer the plot more than grand events do. The romance of the title gathers force quietly, in visits and small services. Readers midway through the set will feel the design: a whole youth built from humble rooms, preparing the joys and regrets that the final volume must settle.
a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-volume-3:
André Theuriet closes his pastoral novel in this third volume. It contains the seventh, eighth, and ninth chapters of the whole. They are The Strange, Dark Secret, Love's Sad Ending, and Love Heals the Broken Heart. Those titles state the book's movement plainly. The secret that has shadowed the heir of Vivey and the woodland queen comes out at last.

Theuriet resolves his tale among the forests where it began, with grief given its full weight before any healing. His strength throughout is place: paths, clearings, and seasons rendered by a writer who knew the Lorraine woods from boyhood. Readers of the earlier volumes will find the loose threads of the unfinished will and the forest loves tied off here.
adela-cathcart-volume-3: George MacDonald continues Adela Cathcart in this third volume, where the contents run from My Uncle Peter continued through The Giant's Heart and A Child's Holiday. Interruption, Percy, The Cruel Painter, The Castle, What Next, Generalship, and An Unforeseen Foresight complete the volume. The first chapter resolves that Chrissy shall tell her uncle her story that evening. A walk together shows her startling at every voice behind her, turning pale, then smiling at herself as a goose.
amelia-volume-3: Henry Fielding's Amelia, volume three, carries Booth and Amelia into the later books of the novel, where Dr. Harrison counsels, strangers appear and town wit is sampled. A masquerade and its consequences, Colonel Bath in great glory and a visit from Captain Trent test the couple's fortunes. The volume closes the Saintsbury edition's Amelia with the history looking backwards before it goes forward.
an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-volume-3:
Neighbors fill An Attic Philosopher in Paris, Volume 3, the third English portion of Emile Souvestre's journal of a poor Paris scholar. The attic floor is a small village: workpeople sharing walls, sounds, and sorrows. Peter the bookbinder's death gives the volume its gravest entry, the philosopher standing by a fellow lodger whose books outlast him. Souvestre writes the funeral of a nobody as an event of state in the republic of the poor.

Inside, the diary keeps its method of meditation tied to errands: a visit, a loan, a small feast, each weighed for what it teaches. The philosopher argues with his own envy when richer men's carriages pass below. Kindness in these pages is work, done on schedule like binding or sewing. Readers in the third volume get the journal's deepest register, grief and gratitude sharing one small room above a Paris most novels never climbed to see.
ancient-records-egypt-breasted-1906-vol-:
Breasted's third volume of Ancient Records, published in 1906, covers the nineteenth dynasty. Seti I and Ramesses II dominate its pages: campaigns in Asia, the great battle of Kadesh, and the peace treaty with the Hittites that followed. Temple inscriptions at Karnak and Abu Simbel supply many of the texts in Breasted's translation.

The Kadesh poems and the treaty text rank among the most studied documents of the ancient world. Later records in the volume trace the dynasty's slow strain under invasion and internal dispute. Breasted arranges all of it with dates, sources, and sober notes. Volume three gives the Ramesside age its full documentary weight. Egypt's voice here is proud, detailed, and increasingly defensive.
andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-military-:
Inside the stockade is where Volume 3 of John McElroy's Andersonville begins, at chapter forty-three. He reflects that no community ever had so little ebb and flow. A city's tides purify it, like the ocean's. The prison's stagnant mass has none. The morning walk, the Rialto where prisoners gather and trade, and the cursing of the Confederacy fill his chapter heads. Between set pieces, an exchanged prisoner tells the story of the battle of Spotsylvania Court House, news from the world of the living.

McElroy writes the middle months: monotony as torture, rumor as currency. Readers deep in the memoir get its hardest truth here. Andersonville killed by inches and by sameness, and this volume's genius is to make the reader feel the sameness without ever being dull.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-3:
Tertullian fills volume three of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, the 1885 set edited by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson. Tertullian of Carthage, writing around 200 AD, was the founder of Latin Christianity's voice. No early writer is fiercer, funnier, or more quotable.

His apologetic works answer pagan slanders and demand fair treatment for Christians before the law. Other treatises rule on prayer, dress, idolatry, and the games, with a rigor that spares no one. Tertullian coined much of the Latin vocabulary of theology, including the word for Trinity. The volume gives the whole of his surviving early work in English dress.
arabian-nights-lane-1877-vol-3:
Volume III of Lane's Thousand and One Nights, in the 1877 printing, completes his pioneering scholarly version. Edward William Lane first issued the work from 1838 to 1840, with drawings and notes drawn from his years in Egypt. The final volume carries Shahrazad's tales to their close in his measured English.

Lane's set taught Victorian Britain to take the Nights seriously as literature and as evidence of Arab life. His omissions are famous, but so is his fidelity where he does translate. Volume III rounds out a version that stands beside Payne's and Burton's as one of the three great English Nights.
arabian-nights-payne-1882-vol-3:
Volume III of Payne's Thousand Nights and One Night, dated 1882, carries the Calcutta text forward in English. The tales turn and turn again: voyages, transformations, and lovers parted by fate and reunited by wit. John Payne's rendering stays complete and unexpurgated, the quality that made his the first full English Nights.

Between Burton's ornate version and Lane's trimmed one, Payne's stands as the full record for its age. Readers who follow the sequence feel the great story-cycle breathing at its own slow, hypnotic pace. Volume III holds the middle of the early nights, with six volumes still to come.
aristophanes-plays-rogers-loeb-1924-vol-:
The third Rogers volume of Aristophanes, published in 1924, completes the Loeb set with Lysistrata, the Thesmophoriazusae, the Ecclesiazusae, and Plutus. In Lysistrata the women of Greece end a war by refusing their husbands until peace is made. Its fame has only grown with the centuries.

The Thesmophoriazusae traps a spy inside a women's festival, mocked in Euripides' own style. The Ecclesiazusae hands Athens to its women, who decree shared property and shared spouses. Plutus, the last play, restores the god of wealth's sight and upends rich and poor. Rogers's rhymes carry the bawdy, topical energy across twenty-four centuries. With this volume the eleven surviving comedies stand complete.
arnold-history-rome-vol-3:
Crisis grips Rome in the third volume of Arnold's History of Rome, from 1838. The Gracchi seek reform, Marius and Sulla march armies on the city, and the free state totters. Arnold, a liberal Englishman, watched ancient liberty die with a keen, wary eye.

He treats the late Republic as a warning for any free people. Wealth, faction, and armed ambition rot the laws from within. Each reform missed makes the next blow worse. His account gains urgency from that parallel, and the volume closes his history with a somber lesson on how republics fall when citizens cease to guard them.
athenaeus-deipnosophists-yonge-vol-3:
Volume three completes Yonge's translation of Athenaeus's Deipnosophists. The banquet of the learned reaches its last courses in this volume. Each dish still sets off cascades of quotation from vanished books.

Slaves, drinking customs, and famous courtesans occupy the later talk. Athenaeus's guests display learning as a competitive sport to the end. The whole work preserves fragments of hundreds of lost Greek writers. Historians of food, music, and daily life mine it constantly. Yonge's three volumes gave English readers the complete ancient feast. Chatty and enormous, the Deipnosophists remains a quarry no classicist can ignore for long.
b09-zwingli-latin-works-3:
The third volume of the Latin Works and Correspondence of Huldreich Zwingli covers 1528 to 1531. Clarence Nevin Heller edited the volume, with introductions by George Warren Richards, in the 1929 Philadelphia issue. The translators of the earlier Jackson edition rendered the Latin texts into English.

Zwingli's last years were his hardest: dispute with Luther over the Lord's Supper, and war clouds over the Swiss cantons. He died in battle at Kappel in 1531, and the correspondence runs to that end. These pages show a reformer holding a city, a pulpit, and a cause at once. The volume completes the standard English record of his Latin works.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-3:
Volume three of Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud holds Tract Erubin, the laws of Sabbath boundaries. Erubin rules seem narrow, but they shape how a whole town keeps the Sabbath together. The 1918 edition continues Rodkinson's twenty-volume translation, the first full English Talmud.

An erub is a shared boundary that lets people carry in public space as if it were one yard. The tractate works out how such boundaries are made: walls, wires, shared food, and joined courtyards. Disputes run over every detail, from a ditch to a leaky wall. The volume shows the rabbis' genius for building community by law.
badauni-muntakhab-vol-3:
Scholars, saints, and poets crowd the third volume of Badauni's Muntakhab, in T. W. Haig's 1899 English version. Rather than battles and decrees, this book offers lives. It forms a kind of who's who of the mind in Akbar's India.

Brief lives trace teachers, mystics, calligraphers, and verse makers of the age. Badauni judges each man by his faith, learning, and character. Praise and blame fall in his usual tart measure. For readers of Mughal culture, the volume is gold: a portrait gallery of a golden age, drawn by a man who knew many of its sitters.
bancroft-history-us-vol-3:
Wars with France shake the colonies in the third volume of Bancroft's History, from 1856. Colonial rights are asserted more boldly as the stakes grow higher each year. The road bends, year by year, toward revolt against Britain.

Bancroft builds his case that liberty was America's birthright from the start. Frontier fights and imperial policy grind against each other in his pages. Assemblies learn to say no, and to mean it. He writes with rising drama here. The stage is set for the crisis volumes that follow in his vast narrative of a people becoming a nation.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-3:
Volume three of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career covers chapters nineteen to twenty-five, the heart of the election. Candidates raise knockers, ring bells, and beg for votes in Bevisham. Nevil's partner Cougham walks where the young hound wants to run. Lord Palmet and certain electors show the borough's price.

A day at Itchincope gives rural relief from the canvass. The examination of the Whigs and a fine blow struck enliven the contest. A drive into Bevisham, a holiday, and an adventure of the boat vary the political grind. Meredith watches democracy at the doorstep, where principles meet beer, bribery, and local pride. Nevil learns his countrymen faster than they learn him. The volume is election reporting raised into comedy and moral study.
bill-s-paper-chase-lady-of-the-barge-and:
W. W. Jacobs places this tale third in The Lady of the Barge and Others, again in the night watchman's voice. Sailormen have their faults, he grants, but closeness with money is seldom among them. He knew one miser in all his years at sea. Thomas Geary shipped aboard the barque Grenada, homeward from Sydney. At sixty he had saved hard for forty years, toward some six hundred pounds.

Geary's hoard, in paper money, becomes the paper chase. Bill and Jimmy quarrel over its hiding place in the fo'c'sle. Bill will take care of it; Jimmy can't trust him. If the place isn't named in a minute, Bill is off to tell the skipper. Jimmy stamps his foot: he hasn't got it, and it's Bill's silly fault. Jacobs builds farce on greed at close quarters.
blundell-s-improvement-odd-craft-part-3:
Blundell's Improvement is a comic short story by W W Jacobs, printed as part three of his Odd Craft set. Jacobs sets the scene at Turnbull's farm, where Venia Turnbull has two suitors calling on a hot Sunday. Sergeant Dick Daly, quick with a compliment, holds the lead.

John Blundell, slow and stubborn, will not leave the room, though Venia's father hints hard at a walk. A trip down to the water gives Blundell his chance to scheme. His odd conduct after that shocks the farm, and he proposes to Miss Sippet on the very day Venia weds him. Jacobs tells it dry and deadpan. Farm courtship, male pride, and a happy muddle make a short, neat tale of manners.
byron-letters-vol-3:
Volume Three of Byron's Letters and Journals, in Prothero's 1898 edition, covers his final years. Byron settled in Italy, wrote his greatest poems, and grew restless for action. The Greek war for independence gave him a cause at last.

The letters trace his life with the Shelleys, the feuds of the Italian years, and the writing of Don Juan. Then comes his sailing for Greece in 1823 to aid the rebels. He died at Missolonghi in 1824, aged thirty-six. This closing volume completes the standard record of Byron's life in his own brilliant words. Prothero closes the set with a full index to all three volumes.
carlyle-cromwell-letters-vol-3:
The Protectorate closes Carlyle's Cromwell in this third volume of the 1904 Lomas edition. Cromwell rules England without a king, facing parliaments, plots, and his own failing health. His death in 1658 ends both the book and an era.

Letters and speeches show triumph turning to loneliness and strain. The great Puritan governs, exhorts, and mourns in his own stark words. Carlyle's devotion to his hero never wavers to the last page. The full set stands as a founding act of Cromwell scholarship. It lets a maligned ruler argue his own case before posterity at last, in full.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-3:
Frederick faces a ring of foes in the third volume of Carlyle's history, in the 1884 printing. The Seven Years' War begins, and Prussia stands against Austria, France, and Russia at once. Defeat stalks the king through his darkest campaigns.

Carlyle tells of endurance raised to the level of tragedy. The great king's genius and grit hold a small state together. Battles turn on hours, and hope on rumor and weather. His devoted English champion spares no detail of the strain. The volume shows hero-worship at its most intense, wedded to research of staggering depth and labor.
carnac-s-folly-volume-3:
Carnac's Folly, Volume 3, by Gilbert Parker, is Book III of the Montreal novel. Parker opens months later, with destiny redrawing the board. Carnac has gone painting at Charlemont with his mother. Tarboe runs the mills successfully. Junia has heard nothing but one letter. It might have been written to a friend, she thinks. A sadness under it troubles her all the same.

A great decision follows, and Carnac becomes a candidate. Junia and Tarboe hear the news. A secret meeting, a challenge, and a blue paper raise the stakes. Denzil takes a hand in the game. A woman writes a letter, and Tarboe has a dream. Halves, Pardner, Halves closes the contents in lumber camp speech. Parker's hero must settle his hidden marriage, his business, and his election together. Canadian politics, in this telling, is another kind of log drive.
cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-volume-:
The third volume of Frances Burney's Cecilia, or Memoirs of an Heiress, brings its heroine's trials toward their close. Book Eight opens with Cecilia scarcely less troubled by her decision than by her doubt, distressed and unhappy with where she stood, what she thought, and herself.

Delvile calls the next morning, fearfully asking his doom with hardly any hope of favour, and Cecilia answers him without affectation or art. Her resolution, and the distress of her long irresolution, drive the volume's emotional centre. Readers who have followed Cecilia through London's routs and snares will find this final volume the most moving of the three.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130005-3:
Memorandum of 1 April 1980 to the Director of Medical Services, from the Psychological Services Staff, revises a table on test reliability. It answers points in the staff's own response to the Inspector General's report on the Professional Applicant Test Battery. A copy of the original Table 1 is attached beside the new version.

Two changes matter, the memo states. An eighth test, Numerical Operations, joins the list examined. Sample sizes also grow almost across the board, taking the total from 426 applicants to 500. Black male numbers rise from 119 to 168, and black females from 79 to 103. White females fall slightly, to 107, because five had not taken the new test. With bigger samples the estimates grow more precise, it notes. For the full group, all eight reliabilities pass the level reported in the text, and half pass a higher one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130014-3:
Memorandum of 31 March 1980 to the Deputy Director for Administration encloses an outside expert's letter on the Inspector General's PATB reports. The writer's name is sanitized throughout. The cover note stresses the letter was not solicited in any way. The Psychological Services chief had offered to write it after reading the reports, it explains.

The sender calls the letter an important companion to the office's fuller rebuttal. He asks that it go to the Inspector General, the Director, and his deputy, as part of the formal response. The letter itself, dated March 24, 1980, is organised in four parts. Its author finds the consultants off the mark on the Strong-Campbell Interest Inventory, and calls their wider concerns those of isolated academics. The whole report was superficial and sloppy, also hostile, he writes. A final part suggests next steps for agency selection policy. Names remain masked under STATINTL marks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100030024-3:
Dated 6 July 1981, a short memorandum to the Chief of the East Asia Division passes on a report of American prisoners of war sighted in Laos. The writer forwards a private letter and asks that the sighting be checked in the field if that has not already been done. Names in the routing account are blacked out in the released copy.

The attached letter, dated 25 May 1981, came from a program manager at a Hmong refugee camp in Thailand. It describes the start of the rainy season after six dry months and the writer's camp work. One passage in it refers to American prisoners seen in Laos, which is why the letter reached the Agency at all.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100070011-3:
A thank-you letter from a former senior officer opens a long file released under a sanitized title. Writing on 13 June 1983, R. Jack Smith tells the editor of Studies in Intelligence that he cannot attend an awards ceremony on 20 June. He thanks the journal board for honoring his essay on Colonel Lawrence K. White.

Smith recalls a retirement party for Sherman Kent and the jokes that carried his farewell speech. The rest of the file is a draft historical essay on the Agency and its overseers. It weighs the wide freedom the CIA was given, the risks that freedom carried, and the slow end of easy congressional trust.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100200002-3:
Draft law to fund aid for Afghanistan is ordered in National Security Directive 5, dated 18 March 1989. Agency routing slips dated 21 March 1989 show the paper moving to the Director, his deputy, and the heads of analysis, operations, and the National Intelligence Council. The directive itself is short and marked confidential.

With Soviet forces leaving Afghanistan, the text expects the Soviet-backed regime to fall and aid to be vital for rebuilding. It directs that draft legislation go to Congress to allow funds and other resources to pass from any department to the Agency for International Development. That agency would lead in drafting and running the program, with other departments in support.
cia-crest-cia-rdp02-06298r000900060006-3:
Level sensors built around displacers are described in a Fisher instruction manual dated May 1980, Form 1802. It covers the caged 249 Series and the Type 259B sensor. The manual gives maintenance steps and parts lists for the sensor alone. Fitting, calibration, and care of the attached controller or transmitter sit in a separate manual.

Type entries distinguish cast iron cages rated at lower pressure classes from steel cages rated higher, with screwed or flanged connections of one and a half or two inches. Cage heads can be turned to eight positions. Maintenance opens with safety steps: drop the vessel level, drain the cage, release pressure, and cut electrical and pneumatic inputs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100090001-3:
Political actors in El Salvador and how they interact are mapped in a secret reference aid dated April 1984, ALA 84-10039. The aid came from the Latin American analysis office with the Office of Global Issues. It rests on information available as of 9 April 1984 and runs to a long, detailed listing.

A summary notes that the military has dominated the country's politics through most of the century, even as it helps move the country in new directions. Party entries follow, with leaders named and origins explained. One entry covers PAISA, a rightist party formed in October 1982 by nine deputies elected that March. Guerrilla plans for urban unrest also appear in the entries.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100360001-3:
Communist and radical leftist influence in Bolivia is the subject of a secret memorandum dated 30 July 1984. The summary dates the rise from the October 1982 start of civilian President Hernan Siles Zuazo's term. Closer ties with Cuba, the Soviet Union, and Nicaragua mark the foreign policy shift it describes.

The paper reports that the pro-Moscow Bolivian Communist Party holds the labor and mining posts in the cabinet. Radical advisers close to Siles are said to be building their own armed forces. Those forces, the paper judges, could not stop a rightist military coup but could carry out disruptive attacks after one. It expects leftist influence to keep growing while Siles stays in office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000100450001-3:
Grenada's first national election in eight years is previewed in a secret memorandum dated 21 November 1984. A deputy assistant secretary of state for Caribbean affairs requested the paper. It rests on information available as of 20 November 1984, ahead of the 3 December vote.

Two opinion polls put the three-party New National Party coalition, led by 66-year-old Herbert Blaize, ahead. The rival Grenada United Labor Party of former prime minister Eric Gairy keeps loyal followers enough for some seats, the paper says. A left party tied to Maurice Bishop's name has little support. The paper also warns that the next government must revive the economy and hold its coalition together.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000201250001-3:
China's improving economic performance is reported in a Directorate of Intelligence memorandum dated 24 February 1984. Gains are clearest in personal consumption and agriculture, the paper says, and economic policy making shows more order and direction. Groundwork for closer economic ties with the West is also noted.

Five years of reform are changing basic ties between the state, the firm, and the individual, the paper argues. It gives a first estimate of 7 percent national income growth for 1983. Yet rapid growth exposes a further need: restructuring the price system. Irrational prices are blamed for shortages, wasted energy, poor quality goods, and swollen costs. Capital equipment imports, up sharply, also figure in the account.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302130002-3:
Thailand's Communist Party after defeat is the subject of a memorandum dated 16 October 1984. The Southeast Asia Division prepared the paper. July arrests of more than 20 party members and several alleged sympathizers open the account, showing that Bangkok still watches the party closely as the rural insurgency fades.

Military fears of urban terrorism or a turn toward the Soviet-aligned Indochinese parties are judged exaggerated. The paper holds that the party is still reeling from four years of government operations and mass defections. A rigid leadership is expected to limit compromise with internal critics or warmer ties abroad. Short-term capacity to build a serious urban network is doubted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302220002-3:
Taiwan's shift away from quiet diplomacy is analyzed in a memorandum dated 14 November 1984. The summary reports that, after three years of a low-key approach, Taipei is moving back to a tougher and more public defense of its international standing. The change has not yet touched ties with the United States.

Hardliners among President Chiang's senior advisers have gained influence, the paper says. They could use American military ties with China to push a loud campaign in Washington on arms and other issues, aimed in part at disrupting ties between Washington and Beijing. Advisers who favor quiet lobbying, such as Fred Chien, would likely oppose that course as dangerous. A sharp reaction from Beijing is expected if hardliners win.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000302230001-3:
United States-China economic relations are the subject of a confidential paper dated 20 November 1984, written as a contribution to an interagency study. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, with a contribution from a Department of Agriculture writer. A release note ties the paper to the Agriculture Department file.

Since a December 1978 party plenum, the paper reports, China has been reshaping and reforming its economy, turning from isolated self-reliance toward wider world involvement. An October 1984 plenum gave the reform program a sweeping endorsement. Many goods would be produced and priced by supply and demand. Joint ventures and co-production with foreign firms are picked out as a prime area of trade growth.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100640001-3:
China's economic reforms are judged in a confidential intelligence assessment dated April 1985, EA 85-10058. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available as of 11 March 1985. Its subtitle pairs performance so far with prospects ahead.

Key judgments say the reform experiment shifted direction and grew sharply in 1984. Where farming had led before, new steps widened the scope. Farmers gained more room for commerce and commodity production. Factories and shops could test new wage programs from April. Rules published soon after let state industrial firms produce goods in short supply once state plans were met. The paper tracks what these openings mean for output and control.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201350001-3:
China's progress in making integrated circuits is measured in a memorandum dated 12 March 1985. The Office of East Asian Analysis produced the paper at the request of a Commerce Department trade official. Building a modern microelectronics industry is named as one of Beijing's primary technology tasks.

Many Chinese circuits are unreliable and wasteful, so Beijing imports most devices needed for key computers and military projects, the summary reports. Chinese output lags the West by about ten years: devices are bigger, use more power, and run more slowly. Weak links include poor coordination between research and production units and scarce test gear. A broad reform of research and a large import program form the reply.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201440001-3:
Japan after the sidelining of Kakuei Tanaka is weighed in a memorandum resting on information available as of 22 March 1985. The Northeast Asia Division prepared the paper. Tanaka, the ruling Liberal Democratic Party's long-time kingpin, suffered a stroke this month.

His fall could shorten Prime Minister Nakasone's tenure and, at worst, crack the party that has governed Japan for thirty years, the paper warns. At best, months of doubt will pull the party's focus from all but the most pressing issues. If Tanaka is lost for good, the roster of Nakasone's backers and rivals will change. The ten-year power struggle around Tanaka would end, bringing a new cast of senior leaders around the prime minister.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302150001-3:
China on the eve of the Vice President's visit is sketched in a memorandum dated 2 October 1985. China Division staff prepared the paper. Deng Xiaoping and other senior leaders should be in a hopeful mood for the visit, the summary reports.

Party meetings in mid-September gave Deng most of his aims. The leadership is younger, better schooled, and more set on economic reform, the paper says. Deng also cut the political weight of the military and of the party's conservative wing. The meetings backed guidelines for the 1986-90 plan that keep market policies in place. A mixed year forms the backdrop: fast industrial growth, inflation, loose credit, and a serious rise in corruption.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302240001-3:
China's September party conference is previewed in a memorandum dated 28 October 1985, EA M 85-10195. The paper sums up the main findings of a study to come, titled China's Party Conference: The Waning of the Ancien Regime. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared both pieces.

From 12 to 24 September the party held a run of meetings without precedent. In two Central Committee sessions and a special conference of delegates, Deng weakened the conservative old guard, the summary reports. He promoted allies to top party bodies and cut the weight of senior military officers. He also won a fresh endorsement of economic reform. A quarter of the 210-member Central Committee is among the figures touched by the changes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05c01629r000100030001-3:
