A first digest point sets a filing rule: a protest of a planned sole-source award must come within 10 days of the notice on FedBizOpps.
gao-gaoreports-b-293925-3:
Poly-Pacific Technologies, Inc., is the protester in GAO decision B-293925.3, dated May 16, 2005. The firm challenged an Air Force award to U.S. Technology Corporation. The contract covered leasing and recycling of abrasive blast media. GAO denied the protest. The agency had fairly judged that the winner's product met the terms of the solicitation. The protester's rival reading of those terms was not a fair one.

At most, the digest says, the protester's reading showed a patent ambiguity in the document. Such a flaw must be protested before award, not after. The solicitation had been a total small business set-aside.
gao-gaoreports-b-294420-3:
Envirosolve's bid for its protest costs is the matter of GAO file B-294420.3, dated February 17, 2005. The Drug Enforcement Administration had sought bids for disposal of hazardous waste seized at clandestine drug laboratories. Envirosolve protested its exclusion from the competitive range. The agency then cancelled the solicitation soon after a supplemental protest was filed. GAO denied the costs. The first protest, it held, was not clearly meritorious.

That finding closed the door under the cost rules. A quick cancellation by the agency does not, on its own, prove that a protest was well founded when it was brought.
gao-gaoreports-b-294572-3:
In GAO files B-294572.3 and B-294572.4, dated October 20, 2005, a protest by Spherix, Inc., is sustained. The Forest Service had awarded ReserveAmerica NY, Inc., the contract for the National Recreation Reservation Service. GAO found that several key points said to justify the award on a cost and technical tradeoff lacked a sound basis. It also found that the agency had misled Spherix on a basic point of compliance. The winner had been praised for offering an alternate start-up plan that broke the stated terms. Spherix had been told the stated plan was required.

This was the second round of the same fight. GAO had sustained Spherix's protest of an earlier award under the same solicitation.
gao-gaoreports-b-294777-3:
Patriot Contract Services is the subject of an advisory opinion in GAO file B-294777.3, dated May 11, 2005. The Navy had awarded American Overseas Marine Corporation a contract to run nine large roll-on and roll-off cargo ships for the military. The solicitation required letters of commitment for key staff. Those letters had to reflect agreed position, salary, and benefits. The record showed that the winner had not in fact discussed salary, benefits, or work location with some of the staff it proposed. On that ground GAO found the protest meritorious.

Because the case came as an advisory opinion, the finding guides the forum that asked for it rather than binding the parties.
gao-gaoreports-b-294867-3:
Manassas Travel, Inc., protested an Army travel contract in GAO file B-294867.3, dated May 3, 2005. The Army had awarded Alexander Travel Ltd. one of six contracts for official travel management. The deals ran two years, with three one-year options. Manassas offered a lower price but drew a weaker risk rating. GAO denied the protest. The award rested fairly on the winner's higher rating under the most heavily weighted technical factor. Named strengths in the record backed that rating.

At a hearing, the agency gave a credible account of those strengths. It matched the written record made at the time. That match let the award stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-294986-3:
Knoll, Inc., and Steelcase, Inc., are the protesters in GAO files B-294986.3 and B-294986.4, dated March 18, 2005. The Air Force had awarded Trade Products Corporation its Total Office Package and Relocation Effort contract. Both furniture makers attacked the scoring of the technical offers. Knoll added a claim about the winner's current schedule contract term. GAO denied the protests. The digest states the ground in one sentence: the record showed that the agency's evaluation was reasonable.

Furniture and office moves may sound minor beside weapons work. The same rules of fair scoring applied, and the same deference to a sound record.
gao-gaoreports-b-295352-3:
Requests by the Department of State and Wackenhut International, Inc., are decided in GAO files B-295352.3 and B-295352.4, dated April 19, 2005. Both sought a second look at a ruling that had sustained Inter-Con Security Systems' protest. The contract covered guard services at the embassy in Abidjan, Ivory Coast. GAO denied the requests for reconsideration. The preference for U.S. persons had been applied without the data the rules required, and nothing showed the agency had that data in time.

The agency's fallback plea fared better. GAO granted a change to its remedy, which had ordered the contract ended at once. Security needs at the embassy and changed needs drove the softer course.
gao-gaoreports-b-295455-3:
In GAO ruling B-295455.3 and B-295455.4, dated August 10, 2005, OTI America, Inc., was the protester. The Government Printing Office was running a limited contest among firms holding parallel contracts for electronic passport book covers. The State Department worked with the printing office on the program. OTI was cut from the contest. GAO denied the protest. A first point confirms that GAO may hear such a case, since the use of options here ran a limited competition.

On the merits, the covers OTI delivered for testing failed material contract terms. That failure gave the agency a sound basis to drop the firm.
gao-gaoreports-b-295496-3:
Poly-Pacific Technologies Inc. returns in GAO file B-295496.3, dated January 18, 2006. The National Guard Bureau had awarded Opti-Blast Inc. a contract for plastic and glass media used to strip paint from Army vehicles, plus recycling of the used media. Poly-Pacific attacked the scoring of the winner's past performance. GAO denied the protest. The digest is one sentence: the agency fairly judged that the contracts cited in the winner's offer were relevant to the work.

Relevance is the hinge of past performance scoring. Work of like kind and scale counts; the agency's call on that point gets deference where the record supports it.
gao-gaoreports-b-296194-3:
TMC Design protested its cut from an Army contest for a jammer system in GAO decision B-296194.3, dated August 10, 2005. The system blocks radio signals that set off roadside bombs. Its name is the CREW System. The firm was cut before field tests of its gear.

GAO denied the protest. The written bid had flaws that field tests could not cure. GAO found that view sound on the record. A bid with deep flaws on paper can be cut early. It need not go to field tests first. The case helps firms see why the written bid must stand on its own.
gao-gaoreports-b-296358-3:
DOR Biodefense and Emergent BioSolutions protested a change to a vaccine deal in GAO decision B-296358.3, dated January 31, 2006. The holder was DynPort Vaccine Company. The work was research on a botulinum vaccine. The Army made the change. The firms said it went past the scope of the first deal.

GAO denied the protests. The change did not shift the type of work in a large way. Cost and time also stayed in the range firms could have seen at first. That kept the change in scope. A change in scope must be large and stark to force a fresh contest. That bar was not met here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296490-3:
Johnson Controls again protested the Treasury guard systems award in GAO decision B-296490.3, dated March 23, 2007. The winner was again Quanta Systems. The site was the currency plant in Washington. This round hit past work marks and staff claims. The agency had missed a key fact on past work.

GAO sustained the protest. The call required past work review. The agency knew how the winner, as the old holder, had done. It failed to weigh that known record. A staff edge claimed for the winner was also weak. The record did not show the agency weighed the firm's own staff plan, which cut the claimed edge.
gao-gaoreports-b-296511-3:
Triad Logistics protested an Air Force award for transient support work in GAO decision B-296511.3, dated October 20, 2005. The winner was M1 Support Services. The site was Mountain Home Air Force Base in Idaho. The buy was set aside for firms owned by disabled veterans. The firm hit past work marks.

GAO denied the protest. The marks fit the scheme in the call. They were also sound on the record. Best value here weighed price and past work. The firm did not show the marks broke that scheme. Past work fights need proof of a flaw in the scheme or the facts. That proof was not made here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296699-3:
BAE Technical Services sought its protest costs in GAO decision B-296699.3, dated August 11, 2006. GAO had backed the firm in its Eglin range fight. The firm sought 488,988.40 dollars. The fight had mixed won and lost points. Proof of how costs split was thin.

GAO backed pay of 463,902.58 dollars. Costs for lost points that stand alone can be cut. Here most cost proof did not split the points well. A page count of the briefs was a sound split tool. That tool set the sum due. The case shows how cost claims are split when briefs mix won and lost claims.
gao-gaoreports-b-296860-3:
Honeywell Technology Solutions sought protest costs in GAO decision B-296860.3, dated December 27, 2005. The first fight was over a Navy award for tech and design support. The winner was Assurance Technology Corporation. A GAO talks track had flagged one point as strong. That point dealt with a clash of roles. The agency then fixed the buy.

GAO split the costs. The agency agreed to pay costs on the flagged point. Other points were never judged in the talks. Those points stood on their own facts. GAO would not back costs for points it had not blessed. Split costs must track the points that drew the fix.
gao-gaoreports-b-296969-3:
JWK International protested an Army award for base support at White Sands in GAO decision B-296969.3, dated January 5, 2006. The winner was C Martin Company. The site was the White Sands Missile Range. The firm claimed bias for the winner. It named the staff lead who ran the buy.

GAO denied the protest. Sworn words from the lead and from peers backed the agency. No proof of bias or bad faith was in the record. The firm did not rebut those sworn words. Bias claims need proof, not mere claims. A bare claim with no facts will fail. The award thus stood on a clean record.
gao-gaoreports-b-297011-3:
Nicholson and Soletanche protested an Army Corps award for dam work in GAO decision B-297011.3, dated April 20, 2006. The winner was Brayman Construction. The site was Bluestone Dam in Hinton, West Virginia. The dam is more than 50 years old. The work would bring it to new safety norms.

GAO denied the protest. Marks fit the call terms and were sound. Tech points in sum far outweighed price in this call. The winner was higher rated on tech. It cost just a bit more. That pick fit the stated weights. When tech far outweighs price, a small price gap will not rule. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297022-3:
Alion Science protested a Defense Information Systems Agency award in GAO decision B-297022.3, dated January 9, 2006. The winner was a unit of ITT Industries. The work was spectrum design help for the Joint Spectrum Center. The winner makes goods that use spectrum bands. Its calls in the work could sway sales of such goods.

GAO sustained the protest. The record did not back the agency view on clash risk. The risk was at its peak here, not low. The winner would make calls that could help or hurt its own goods and rival goods. That clash needed a deep check. The check made was too thin to stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-297077-3:
The Environmental Protection Agency sought a fresh look at the furniture case in GAO decision B-297077.3, dated January 25, 2006. GAO had backed Haworth over a deal for Herman Miller. The site was Potomac Yard in Crystal City, Virginia. The agency said GAO read the contest rules too strictly.

GAO denied the request. When an agency runs a contest under the schedule plan, it sets terms and tests in a call. It must then live by those terms and tests. It cannot brush them aside at the pick stage. That rule held here. The first ruling thus stood with no change.
gao-gaoreports-b-297133-3:
ManTech Security Technologies protested a State Department award in GAO decision B-297133.3, dated April 24, 2006. The winner was Siemens Government Services. The work was design and tech help for guard gear. That gear guards State sites round the world. The firm hit crowd size at talks, weak point talks, and marks.

GAO denied the protest. A rival firm had more than 10 staff at its talk. That fact did not harm this firm. The winner had just 10 staff there. Weak spots that came from side-by-side review need not be raised in talks. Marks fit the call tests and were sound. The pick thus stood on a fair record.
gao-gaoreports-b-297177-3:
NANA Services protested a Navy bridge deal for morale services on Guam in GAO decision B-297177.3, dated January 3, 2006. The holder was Global Food Services. The deal sat in the 8(a) small firm program. It was made with no contest. The work held child care, youth help, sport, and book services. Staff on the far isle need such help.

GAO denied the protest. The take of the need into the 8(a) plan broke no law or rule. That take was the base for the no-contest deal. Once the need was in the plan in a lawful way, the bridge could be set. The firm showed no bar in law to that path.
gao-gaoreports-b-297200-3:
Global Analytic protested the terms of an Army call for program help in GAO decision B-297200.3, dated March 21, 2006. The work backed Army upkeep software refits. The call first was set aside for small firms. It was then run with no set-aside. The firm, a small firm, said the set-aside should stay.

GAO denied the protest. Set-aside rules do not bind schedule buys in the same way. The agency could lift the set-aside for this buy. That lift was not flawed. Small firms can still bid in an open schedule buy. No right to a set-aside held here. The open call thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297252-3:
TruLogic protested an Air Force award for tech manual systems in GAO decision B-297252.3, dated January 30, 2006. The winner was Command Technology. The work held growth of digital tech manuals and upkeep of tech orders. The firm hit tech and price marks. It also claimed the pick lead was biased.

GAO denied the protest. The pick lead set aside the bulk of the scorers. She took the view of the few. That step was fine here. She gave a clear cause, backed by the record. She found the low priced bid merited a higher tech mark and was best value. A lead may differ from staff when she shows her work. No bias was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-297397-3:
New England Radiation Therapy sought protest costs in GAO decision B-297397.3, dated February 2, 2006. The first fights hit a Veterans Affairs award for radiation therapy. The site was the VA Medical Center in Providence, Rhode Island. The winner was Radiation Oncology Associates. The firm said the agency fixed the buy due to its first protest.

GAO denied the request. Costs need a protest that was clearly strong. This first protest was not shown to be clearly strong. Even if the fix did track the protest, that link is not enough. Weak claims do not earn costs when an agency opts to fix a buy. The claim thus failed on strength.
gao-gaoreports-b-297450-3:
Saturn Landscape protested Air Force acts on grounds work in Alaska in GAO decision B-297450.3, dated April 18, 2006. The site was Eielson Air Force Base. The firm claimed bad faith at each step. Steps hit were the axing of the first call, a new call with a HUBZone set-aside, and posts that it called sly.

GAO denied the protest. No base was shown to doubt the acts. The first call was axed to cut option years and shift tests. That was a sound cause. The set-aside rested on a fair hope of two or more HUBZone bids at fair prices. Bad faith needs proof. None was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-297648-3:
Yardney Technical Products sought protest costs in GAO decision B-297648.3, dated March 28, 2006. The first fight hit an Air Force award for space-grade batteries. The winner was Quallion. The work sought a home source for lithium-ion cells for space craft. The agency fixed the buy after the protest. The firm sought its costs on that base.

GAO denied the request. The protest was not clearly strong. More facts and deep work would have been due to solve it. Costs track protests that were clearly strong on their face. A hard, close case that needs deep work does not meet that bar. A fix by the agency alone does not earn costs.
gao-gaoreports-b-297758-3:
JWK International protested its loss in the fuels work re-run in GAO decision B-297758.3, dated August 31, 2006. The site was Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio. A prior protest by United Paradyne had forced a fresh review. The firm hit past work marks. It said key staff skill should count, and that its sub firm's top work proved it could do the job.

GAO denied the protest. The agency had a sound base to skip staff skill in past work marks. Past work grades the firm, not each hire. Top work by a sub firm on part of the job did not prove the lead firm could run the full job well. That view was sound.
gao-gaoreports-b-297800-3:
Skyline ULTD protested the rejection of its bid for tech work in GAO decision B-297800.3, dated August 22, 2006. The buyer was the General Services Administration. The bid missed a note to mark a change to the call. The firm said the change was small. It sought to have the miss waived as a slip.

GAO denied the protest. The change held key terms on the legal tie of the sides. It set a duty to watch for shifts in travel risk zones abroad. It also set a duty to flag such shifts fast to the agency. Terms of that weight are not small. A missed note for a key change cannot be waived.
gao-gaoreports-b-297838-3:
The Arora Group protested a Navy award for radiology support in GAO decision B-297838.3, dated September 12, 2006. The winner was STG International. The site was the Naval Medical Center in Portsmouth, Virginia. The buy was set aside for small firms. The firm hit past work marks for the bids. The winner was higher rated and lower priced.

GAO denied the protest. Marks fit the call terms and were sound. The call sought the most strong bid in full. The winner was that bid on both tech and price. A pick that wins on both counts is hard to undo. No flaw in past work marks was shown that would shift the result.
gao-gaoreports-b-297950-3:
Propper International protested a Defense Logistics Agency award for camo gear in GAO decision B-297950.3, dated March 19, 2007. The winner was Tennier Industries. The goods were all-purpose camo parkas and trousers. The firm had made and helped grow those goods in the past. It hit past work marks and the pick. The winner cost a bit more and scored higher.

GAO denied the protest. Marks and the pick fit the call terms and were sound. Tries to reach past work peers for the firm were judged fair. Past skill with the goods did not force a win. A small price gap does not beat a higher tech score when the review is sound.
gao-gaoreports-b-298047-3:
Family Entertainment Services protested an Army award for grounds work in GAO decision B-298047.3, dated September 20, 2006. The winner was Total Grounds Maintenance. The site was Fort Campbell, Kentucky. The buy was set aside for HUBZone firms. The firm hit past work marks. Tries to reach its past peers were thin, it said.

GAO sustained the protest. The agency tried hard to reach the winner's peers. It tried far less for the firm's peers. That split was unfair. Notes also gave no clear cause for the firm's past work marks. Score sheets on file were not weighed in a clear way. Past work review must be even and well writ.
gao-gaoreports-b-298099-3:
Overlook Systems sought protest costs in GAO decision B-298099.3, dated October 5, 2006. The first fight hit an Air Force award for GPS center help. The site was Schriever Air Force Base in Colorado. The winner was LinQuest Corporation. Claims held clash fears, marks, and the pick. The agency fixed the buy in part.

GAO denied the request. The protests were not clearly strong. Costs need a clearly strong protest when an agency opts to fix a buy. Close claims on clash and marks do not meet that bar. A fix step alone does not prove the claims were strong. The cost plea thus failed on strength.
gao-gaoreports-b-298333-3:
Raith Engineering protested an Army award for fuel support in Kuwait in GAO decision B-298333.3, dated January 9, 2007. The winner was Kellogg Brown and Root Services. The work was fuel help at two sites. The firm had first filed a protest with the agency. That first filing came late. Timing thus barred the GAO case at the gate.

GAO dismissed the protest. A GAO case that rests on a late agency case will not be heard. The agency filing came more than 10 days after a full brief was given. That brief gave the facts for a protest. Firms must file at agency level in 10 days from such a brief, or lose the GAO path.
gao-gaoreports-b-298380-3:
Avue Technologies Corp. and Carahsoft Technology Corp. protested terms in a solicitation for the Department of Homeland Security. The Internal Revenue Service ran the buy for DHS. The contract sought a system to automate staff recruitment and hiring. GAO decided the case, B-298380.3, on November 15, 2006.

The firms attacked clauses on data rights in the solicitation. They also faulted the way price would be judged. GAO found the clauses only guard the government's rights in its own hiring data. It also found the fixed-price plan judged cost in a fair way. No rule required credit for side savings in agency staff costs. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298394-3:
Phyllis M. Chestang protested the lack of an award under a Small Business Administration solicitation. The buy sought home and business loan processing to aid disaster recovery work. Awards would run one base year plus four option years. GAO decided B-298394.3 on November 20, 2006.

The agency scored Chestang's proposal as poor overall. GAO found that score fair. The proposal left out facts the solicitation had asked for by name. Those facts were needed for the agency to judge the offer. A thin proposal could not support a claim of flawed review. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298432-3:
Indtai Inc. protested Army awards of three contracts for education support services. The work aids staff who teach adult education at sites in eight regions worldwide. Awards were to rest on best value. GAO decided B-298432.3 on January 17, 2007.

Indtai faulted the way the Army judged the offers. GAO upheld two key points of that review. First, the past record of named subcontractors could count toward an offeror's score. The terms did not bar that step. Second, the Army's price check was enough for this buy. It found prices fair through real price rivalry. No deeper realism check was owed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298682-3:
Global Solutions Network, Inc. protested the Army's award on the HRsolutions buy a third time. The contract went to Accurate Conceptions, LLC. The work covered task order management and financial support. GAO decided B-298682.3 and B-298682.4 on June 23, 2008.

The firm faulted the scoring and called the winner's price too low. GAO found the scoring sound in most respects. Two flaws it noted caused the firm no real harm. Late past-record facts and extra resume pages did not sway the result. On price, a third firm bid a like sum. That match made the low price look fair. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298720-3:
Midland Supply, Inc. returned with a second protest of the same General Services Administration award. The contract again went to Danaher Tool Group for socket wrench sets. The agency had redone its best-value call after the first ruling. GAO decided B-298720.3 on May 14, 2007.

The redo failed on a key factor. On-time delivery records weighed heavily in the pick. GAO found the new call misstated how the two firms' records compared. That error struck at the heart of the trade-off. A best-value call must rest on true facts about the offers. GAO sustained the protest again.
gao-gaoreports-b-298865-3:
Team BOS/Naples--Gemmo /DelJen protested a Navy award on the same Naples base operations buy. This time the contract went to the Italian joint venture it had beaten in a prior round. GAO decided B-298865.3 on December 28, 2007.

The firm attacked the scoring of technical and price offers. It also claimed the price realism review was too thin. GAO found the review fair and backed by the record. The pick memo held some errors, the firm noted. The agency showed those slips did not sway the core logic. A sound core can stand past small memo flaws. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298866-3:
The Salvation Army Community Corrections Program sought payment of its protest costs. The plea grew from a Federal Bureau of Prisons buy. The contract covered Comprehensive Sanctions Center services for offenders. GAO acted in B-298866.3, a costs ruling, on August 29, 2007.

GAO backed the claim in full. The protest had been clearly sound on its merits. Yet the agency was slow to take its fix. Such delay in the face of a strong protest can support a cost award. GAO also treated the scoring claims as one linked whole. Costs for both won and lost points could be paid. It backed payment of the fair costs.
gao-gaoreports-b-298870-3:
Axiom Resource Management, Inc. protested a task order to Lockheed Martin Federal Healthcare, Inc. The order covered program management support for the TRICARE Acquisitions Directorate. The Army Medical Research Acquisition Activity ran the buy. GAO ruled in B-298870.3 and B-298870.4 on July 12, 2007.

The firm claimed a conflict of interest tainted the order. GAO reviewed the agency's check of current and future work. The agency found no clash in current deals. It judged that future risks could be eased. The winner would also be barred from later health-benefit award work. That plan was fair on the record. GAO denied the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-298872-3:
Frontier Systems Integrators, LLC protested a Navy award to Chenega Security and Protection Services, LLC. The contract covered security guard services at Naval Station Newport in Rhode Island. The Naval Facilities Engineering Command ran the buy. GAO decided B-298872.3 on February 28, 2007.

The firm faulted how the winner's record was judged. The winner's parent firm had a guard record of its own. But the parent's role was limited to back-office support. GAO let the agency keep the two apart. A second claim faulted a thin set of past-record forms. That point went to fitness, which was not attacked. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298880-3:
MASAI Technologies Corporation protested an Army award to Denysys Corporation. The buy sought computer and technical support for a medical logistics system. That system is the Theater Wide Enterprise Logistics System. GAO ruled in B-298880.3 and B-298880.4 on September 10, 2007.

The agency judged the firm's proposal short on staff credentials. The terms set clear bars for staff skill. GAO found the low mark well grounded. The firm also claimed the winner held an unfair edge. The agency had probed both firms' past work for clashes. That probe backed its clean call. No unfair edge was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299091-3:
AdaRose, Inc. protested an Army move to raise bars in a solicitation. The buy covered armaments software engineering center support. The Army Joint Armaments Contracting Center ran the contest. GAO ruled in B-299091.3 on March 28, 2008.

The new terms asked for deep grasp of agency software design methods. The firm called that bar an undue curb on rivalry. GAO found the bar tied to real work needs. Staff who know the design path can do the work well. A term tied to true needs can stand. The firm also faulted a past score shown as an aid. That score was not a fresh review. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299307-3:
Panacea Consulting, Inc. sought payment of protest costs from the Department of Labor. The plea grew from protests of delivery orders to Systems Integration and Development, Inc. Those orders covered project management and research support services. GAO acted in the B-299307 costs ruling on July 24, 2007.

The agency had taken a fix after a GAO-led settlement talk. GAO backed cost payment in part. Payment tracks the points on which a firm prevails. Some winning points rested on facts apart from the lost points. Those apart costs could be split off and paid. Linked costs stayed bound to their own fate. GAO backed payment to that extent.
gao-gaoreports-b-299322-3:
Optimum Management Systems, LLC protested an Interior Department award path for financial systems support. The agency ended the firm's contract and picked SofTec Solutions, Inc. instead. The work serves the National Business Center. The contest ran as an 8(a) set-aside. GAO ruled in B-299322.3 on May 23, 2007.

SofTec bid lower on price with a lower score. The firm held the higher score at a higher price. GAO found the trade-off fair. The agency judged the added cost of the top score not worth paying. That premium call is the core of best-value work. It rested on a sound view of both bids. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299366-3:
Benchmade Knife Company protested a Defense Logistics Agency award to Gerber Legendary Blades. The contract covered two combat knives. Scores came in part from an automated best value system. GAO ruled in B-299366.3 and B-299366.4 on July 16, 2007.

The case grew from a redo of the scoring. The firm said the agency used a fresh time span for the winner's score. That span would sweep in newer delivery facts. GAO read the record for proof. It found the agency used the same scores in both rounds. The first marks, not new ones, drove the redo. No term breach was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299486-3:
Liberty Street East Associates protested an Agriculture Department lease award in Warren, Pennsylvania. The space would host the Allegheny National Forest Supervisor's Office. The lease went to Ashford/Warren Associates, LP. GAO ruled in B-299486.3 on June 15, 2007.

Some claims died by silence. The agency's report rebutted the price claims. The firm sent no reply to that rebuttal. Claims left unanswered count as dropped. Later side notes could not revive them. The scoring claims also failed on harm. Even at the firm's claimed score, the winner scored higher. Its lower price sealed the same result. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299504-3:
The Environmental Protection Agency and CGI Federal asked GAO to void a prior ruling. That ruling had backed an IBM protest over a financial system upgrade award. Later events, they said, changed the case. GAO acted in B-299504.3 and B-299504.4 on July 23, 2008.

GAO refused to undo its call. A plea to vacate needs strong new proof. The movers had to show the ruling was now invalid. Or they had to show the public interest would gain from a void. Neither showing was made on this record. Later shifts alone do not erase a sound ruling. GAO denied the reconsideration requests.
gao-gaoreports-b-299542-3:
AT&T Corp. protested a Social Security Administration award to Nortel Government Solutions. The contract covered a telephone systems replacement project. The agency runs a staff of more than 65,000 across the country. GAO ruled in B-299542.3 and B-299542.4 on November 16, 2007, with a split result.

Talks on the firm's staffing plan fell short. The agency found deep flaws in that plan. It then failed to show the firm how wide those worries ran. A second flaw hit the winner's score. Later calls clashed with the first findings, with no account of the shift. On other points, the firm's claims failed. GAO sustained the protest in part.
gao-gaoreports-b-299556-3:
Diligent Consulting sought payment of protest costs from the Air Force. The plea grew from protests over software support services at Maxwell Air Force Base. The agency took a fix and pledged to rescore the bids. GAO acted in B-299556.3, a costs ruling, on June 26, 2007.

Cost payment needs a clearly sound protest. The firm's first protest did not meet that bar. Its added protest drew a swift fix from the agency. A fast fix cuts against a cost award for that round. The firm claimed the agency dragged its feet. The record showed a prompt path once the new points landed. GAO denied the request.
gao-gaoreports-b-299595-3:
J&J Colombia Services MV LTDA protested an Army sole-source award in Colombia. The interim deal went to PAE Colombia LTDA for logistics support services. The work serves a U.S. Military Group in Bogota and sites nationwide. GAO decided B-299595.3 on June 26, 2007.

The firm blamed poor advance planning for the sole-source path. GAO weighed the facts on the ground. A long-term award for the same work sat held up by court fights. The services were needed at once, with no gap allowed. The prior firm was the sole one placed to step in fast. Urgent need on that proof can back a short sole-source deal. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299821-3:
Eagle Home Medical Corporation sought payment of protest costs from the Veterans Affairs Department. The plea grew from a protest over a buy for oxygen supplies and services. That work serves veterans at the Atlanta medical center. GAO acted in B-299821.3, a costs ruling, on February 4, 2008.

GAO backed the cost claim in full. The protest had been clearly sound on its merits. It urged that the buy be set aside for small firms. Yet the agency waited to act. It took its fix only after its report and the firm's notes were filed. Such delay in the face of a strong claim can support payment. GAO backed the fair costs.
gao-gaoreports-b-299954-3:
Executive Protective Security Service protested a Federal Emergency Management Agency task order in Mississippi. The order went to Security Consultants Group for armed guard services. The guards watch FEMA housing sites in that state. GAO ruled in B-299954.3 on October 22, 2007.

Eligibility again turned on the Stafford Act. The agency found the winner did business chiefly in Mississippi. GAO weighed that call against the record. The facts did not back a chief-in-state base for the firm. A set-aside tied to local firms needs a true local tie. The agency's call stretched past what the proof showed. That flaw tainted the task order pick. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-309972-3:
Deva & Associates PC lost its protest. GAO decided B-309972.3 on April 29, 2008. The Education Department had sought accounting help. It then killed its call for quotes and planned a fresh race. The firm said the kill lacked a fair basis. The work mixed books work with credit reform reports.

GAO denied the protest. The agency's needs had shifted in clear ways. Books work for small firms had shrunk. Credit reform work had grown a lot. The agency meant to join all the work in one task order. That order would still be set aside for small firms. Shifting needs can back a fresh race.
gao-gaoreports-b-309999-3:
Capitol Supply, Inc. lost its protest under GAO decision B-309999.3, dated January 22, 2008. The General Services Administration sought office goods for many agencies. It asked schedule firms to quote for blanket buy deals. The goods ran from pens to toner and paper. Capitol Supply was cut from the race at the start.

GAO held the cut was proper. The firm failed to heed firm price rules in the call. Those rules were a must, not a tip. A quote that skips a must can be set aside at once. The case warns firms to read price rules with great care.
gao-gaoreports-b-310331-3:
Lakeside Escrow & Title Agency, Inc. lost its protest. GAO decided B-310331.3 on January 7, 2008. The Housing and Urban Development office sought home closing services in Michigan. The work ties to homes lost on backed loans. Lakeside was cut from the lead pack of bids. It fought the tech score that drove the cut.

GAO denied the protest. The score and the cut were both fair. Each fit the points the call set out. A firm cut from the pack must show the score broke the call's terms. Mere clash with the score is not enough. Close calls in scoring sit with the agency.
gao-gaoreports-b-310340-3:
McGoldrick Construction Services Corporation lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-310340.3, dated May 16, 2008. The Veterans Affairs office sought build services at its San Antonio hospital. The work spans core build trades and fire safety systems. It also covers asbestos and lead cleanup. The award went to Strategic Perspectives Development, LLC.

GAO denied the protest. The file showed fair scores and a fair pick. Both fit the call's terms and the rules of the buy game. The loser showed no flaw that would shift the result. A sound file beats a loser's clash of views on scores.
gao-gaoreports-b-310372-3:
Pemco Aeroplex, Inc. lost its new protest (GAO decision B-310372.3, dated June 13, 2008). The Air Force had fixed its KC-135 depot care pick after a past GAO ruling. That ruling told the agency to run and write down a price test. The agency did so and kept Boeing as the pick. Pemco fought the fix as thin.

GAO denied the protest. The agency need not reopen talks to run the price test. Its file wrote down its calls on cost and risk in clear terms. Those notes back the pick in a fair way. A cure that heeds a GAO fix can stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-310454-3:
Protest costs are refused in this GAO decision, B-310454.3, dated March 27, 2008. Singleton Enterprises-GMT Mechanical, Joint Venture had fought a Veterans Affairs roof buy. The agency gave in and fixed the flaw. The firm then asked for its protest costs back. It said a like past win meant this fight should not have been needed.

GAO denied the cost claim. The agency missed its report date, it is true. But it told of its fix just 2 days past that date. That pace counts as fair speed in GAO's view. The firm had not yet had to draft its reply to a report. Small cost, fast fix: no pay-back is due.
gao-gaoreports-b-310600-3:
Protest costs are granted in this GAO decision, B-310600.3, dated June 5, 2008. Two firms had fought an Army award for laundry services at camps in Kuwait. The award had gone to a Kuwait firm. The call asked for the low bid at a price judged real. The firms said no true price test was run. They then asked for their protest costs back.

GAO granted the cost claims. A fair first check by the Army would have shown the flaw. The price test the call asked for was never run. Yet the Army stalled its fix past its report date. A plain flaw plus a late fix leaves the agency owing costs.
gao-gaoreports-b-310661-3:
Karrar Systems Corporation lost a fresh protest in GAO decision B-310661.3, dated March 3, 2008. The case picks up the Army R2 program buy. Karrar had lost to BANC3, Inc. in the first round. It now fought the winner's pass mark. That mark came with eight weak points and three strong ones. Karrar also fought its own mid mark and a 30 percent price gap.

GAO denied the protest. A pass mark need not rest on a count of plus and minus points. The pick chief weighed each point and the facts beneath the marks. A top tech bid may still lose if its price premium is too steep.
gao-gaoreports-b-310737-3:
Native American Industrial Distributors, Inc. won part of its protest. GAO decided B-310737.3 on April 15, 2008. The buy ran as a set-aside under the Buy Indian Act. One claim hit the winner's class claim. The winner is a unit of an Alaska Native firm. No Native staff hold top posts in the firm. The loser said that fact barred the win.

GAO split its ruling. The class claim held up, since the call set no firm test and the Act can be read to let the firm in. But the win broke a clear term. The call asked for pledge notes from all key staff. The winner sent none for some posts. That flaw sustained the protest in part.
gao-gaoreports-b-311314-3:
New Jersey & H Street, LLC won its protest. That ruling is B-311314.3, dated June 30, 2008. The case is a twin of a lease fight in Washington. The General Services Administration sought space for the Justice Department. The winner's block got marks for perks to come. Proof for those perks was a bare word in the bid. The call had asked for firm proof from a third hand.

GAO sustained the protest. The proof rule was bent for the winner alone. This firm got no chance to bid perks on the soft rule. Talks missed big flaws on perks near its own block as well. Soft rules for one side warp a race.
gao-gaoreports-b-400168-3:
Protest costs are refused in this GAO decision, B-400168.3, dated August 18, 2008. Brian X. Scott had fought an Army call for staff aid in Iraq. The call dealt with aid for jail work by troops. The Army gave in and fixed the flaw in its call. Scott then asked for his protest costs back. He said the fix came past the first due date for the Army's report.

GAO denied the cost claim. GAO had in fact let the Army have more time for its report. The Army told of its fix before that report was filed. A fix on a path GAO set is no undue lag. Costs need a lag the file can show.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-3:
Military dining contracts under two jobs programs are compared in GAO report GAO-08-3, dated October 30, 2007. Two federal programs turn contracts into work for people with disabilities. In 2006, their dining deals with the Defense Department were worth $465 million a year. A 2007 defense law ordered this study.

One program trains blind vendors, through state agencies, to run dining halls. Most of its contracts pair the vendor with a commercial food firm. The other program works through nonprofit agencies. GAO contrasted how each side wins contracts and sets prices. It also compared what the workers themselves are paid. State surveys and 14 contracts ground the account.
gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrated-boo:
Book 3 of Rabelais's giant tale, in the English version begun by Sir Thomas Urquhart, finds Panurge rich with questions and poor in answers. He has spent his money and now asks one thing: should he marry, and will his wife stay true? Pantagruel listens, jokes, and sends him from one wise source to the next.

Panurge asks poets, doctors, judges, fools, and churchmen, and each reply can be read two ways. Dreams and lots give no firm word. The quest turns each kind of learned talk into sport, as Rabelais mocks law, medicine, and fate-telling alike. The book ends with the pair set to seek a last oracle by sea, which drives the next book's voyage.
gellius-attic-nights-rolfe-loeb-vol-3:
The Attic Nights of Aulus Gellius closes with books fourteen through twenty in this third Loeb volume, translated by John C. Rolfe. Gellius wrote his notebook of Roman lore in the second century, for his children and for readers like them. The last books bring the twenty-book miscellany to its end.

Star lore, old laws, word histories, and tales of philosophers fill these pages. Gellius keeps quoting lost authors, and each quote is a small rescue from oblivion. His own voice stays modest and eager, a friend showing you his shelves. The full set preserves more lost Latin prose than any other single book of its age.
gerfaut-volume-3:
Charles de Bernard tightens his love plot in Gerfaut, Volume 3 of the English edition. Octave de Gerfaut, now a famous writer, moves in the Bergenheim circle as an honored guest. The baroness draws the devotion he once spent on fame. Bernard writes the attraction from inside the man's mind.

Visits and country amusements give the pair cover for a feeling neither names plainly. The Baron watches his house with a host's smile and a husband's suspicion. Marillac and Mademoiselle de Corandeuil sharpen the comedy around the pair. Bernard keeps every scene proper on its surface and dangerous underneath. Hunts and dinners supply the accidents through which secrets leak. Readers in the third volume feel the design closing: a marriage of rank, a guest of genius, and an affection needing one careless hour to become a scandal.
godolphin-volume-3:
At chapter twenty-two, the third volume finds the bride alone. Constance is now Countess of Erpingham, in the first months of her marriage, alone in a splendid room while London adores rank and wealth outside. A chapter head praises her genius for diplomacy and the character of her assemblies, where she conquers even Lady Delville.

Marriage has given Constance a stage, not happiness. Her talks turn on politics and matches while her heart stays fixed on Godolphin, now lost to her by her own choice. Lytton shows the glitter and the ache of a great lady's life in one portrait. This middle volume deepens the novel's study of what the world gives, and what it takes.
good-intentions-ship-s-company-part-3:
W. W. Jacobs made his name with tales of the London docks, told by a night-watchman with a dry tongue. Good Intentions is the third part of Ship's Company, his linked set of comic stories. It opens with the watchman's broom found lashed to a crane top at the jetty end, bristles to the sky. The watchman is sure he knows the culprit: jealousy, pure jealousy.

He tells how jealousy has dogged him since his marriage, with his wife setting traps and friends blackening his name. Jacobs writes the talk of the wharves exactly, with its dropped letters and sly turns. The humor is gentle and the plots are small, built on vanity, drink, and courtship. These tales were loved in their day and still give a warm hour by the river of print.
hallam-constitutional-history-vol-3:
Restoration to George the Second fills the third volume of Hallam's Constitutional History, from 1827. The Glorious Revolution expels James the Second and settles the crown by law. The Bill of Rights then fixes limits that kings must not cross.

Hallam completes his great argument in this closing book. England's constitution appears as the slow triumph of law over arbitrary power. Parties, parliaments, and courts settle into their modern shapes here. His judgments shaped a century of political thought and debate. The full work remains a founding text of Whig history, prized for learning, balance, and quiet moral force.
hallam-middle-ages-vol-3:
Towns, trade, and learning close Hallam's medieval survey in this third volume, from 1860. Cities grow rich and free as feudal bonds loosen across Europe. Schools revive old learning, and the first light of a new age appears on many horizons.

Hallam ends his great work where the modern world begins. He traces the institutions that would shape all that followed after. Commerce, law, and letters rise together in his final chapters. The three volumes form a pioneering survey in English. They taught their century to see the Middle Ages as the seedbed of modern Europe, not its dark prelude.
hawkesworth-account-voyages-southern-hem:
The third volume of Hawkesworth's Account of the Voyages, from 1773, closes the official set. It carries Cook's first voyage in the Endeavour to its end: the charting of New Zealand, the east coast of Australia, and the wreck on the Great Barrier Reef. It also looks ahead to Cook's second voyage, then fitting out.

The Endeavour's near-loss on the reef, and her crew's fight to save her, makes gripping reading. Botany Bay, named for Banks's plants, enters the map here. Hawkesworth's smooth first-person blend of Cook's and Banks's journals drew fire for liberties taken. Even so, the three volumes fixed the Pacific in Europe's imagination.
hinduism-and-buddhism-an-historical-sket:
Charles Eliot closes his historical sketch with this third volume. The set traces Hinduism and Buddhism from their Indian roots. By this volume the story has spread far beyond India. Eliot follows Buddhism's long road east and north across Asia.

Chapters treat the faith under China's T'ang dynasty and its later heirs. Eliot weighs courts, monks, and wars as the faith rose and fell. Spelling notes explain how names from many tongues are rendered. Readers who finish the set gain a wide survey of two great faiths across Asia, written in a clear and measured style.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's third volume, with Milman's notes, begins at chapter twenty-seven with the reign of Theodosius and the civil wars against Maximus and Eugenius. The ruin of Arianism, Saint Ambrose, and Theodosius's public penance fill the opening movement. Chapter twenty-eight then narrates the final destruction of paganism under Christian emperors.

Later chapters cover the Gothic invasions, Alaric's sack of Rome, Attila and the Huns, and the last western emperors, ending near chapter thirty-eight. Persian wars in Mesopotamia, where a martial bishop defends his city, show Gibbon's range. The volume carries Rome from a still-mighty Christian empire to the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in the west.
humboldt-cosmos-otte-vol-3:
The third volume of Humboldt's Cosmos, in Otté's English translation, returns to the heavens with the tools of mature astronomy. Humboldt planned the work as a physical description of the universe, and this volume treats the celestial half in depth. It followed volumes one and two in the Bohn edition of 1849.

Stars, double stars, nebulae, and the solar system's planets and comets pass in ordered review. Humboldt weighs what the telescope had proven by mid-century and marks the open questions plainly. His care to separate fact from guess made Cosmos a model of honest popular science. The volume also holds his thoughts on the light and heat of the sun.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
The third volume of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Williams's translation, came out in 1818. It carries the expedition down its boldest line: the Orinoco river system. Humboldt set out to prove the Orinoco joins the Amazon through the Casiquiare canal, a link geographers doubted.

By canoe, through clouds of biting insects, the party runs rapids and portages into the Rio Negro. Humboldt confirms the canal with his own instruments, redrawing the map of a continent. He records missions, river peoples, and the poisons and medicines of the forest. The volume is the heart of the whole Narrative, where his fame as an explorer was made.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-3:
Brand preaches all or nothing, and the demand slowly destroys everyone he loves. Ibsen's towering verse drama fills the third volume of Archer's English edition, in C. H. Herford's translation, published in 1908. A young priest in a mountain parish refuses every compromise the world offers him.

The play became a sensation across Scandinavia, argued over in pulpits and newspapers alike. Brand's purity inspires and horrifies in equal measure, which is the tragedy's engine. Is he a saint of integrity or a fanatic drunk on his own will? Ibsen never answers cleanly. The work stands as his most uncompromising statement, a tragedy of idealism itself.
ihne-history-rome-vol-3:
Carthage and Rome collide in the third volume of Ihne's History, from 1871. Hannibal crosses the Alps and wins at Cannae, Rome's darkest day of the age. Scipio answers by carrying the war to Africa itself and ending it at Zama.

Ihne tells the titanic struggle with clarity and gripping pace. Two great republics fight for mastery of the western Mediterranean world. His chapters balance strategy, politics, and the temper of each people. Few accounts of the Punic Wars match its order and force. The volume stands among the clearest ever written on the war that made Rome a world power.
isbe-1915-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Orr's International Standard Bible Encyclopedia came out in 1915 with the rest of the set. The encyclopedia aimed to give Bible readers a complete reference that joined sound scholarship to traditional faith. By the third volume, the undertaking was in mid-course, the alphabet well advanced.

More of the ancient world is recovered here, and more of Scripture's background explained, article by signed article. The steady, learned progress of Orr's project shows on every page: maps, lists, and long treatments of major topics beside short notes on small names. The set became the standard Bible dictionary of its age for conservative readers. Volume 3 keeps the standard through the middle of the alphabet, and students of the period still consult it for the state of knowledge in 1915.
jack-sheppard-a-romance-vol-1-of-3:
William Harrison Ainsworth issued Jack Sheppard in three volumes in 1839, and this is volume one. Epoch one, 1703, follows Jonathan Wild from the widow and her child. Mr. Wood offers to adopt little Jack Sheppard in the illustrations list. Wild discovers Darrell in a loft, and a murder on the Thames follows.

Epoch two opens in 1715 with the idle apprentice. Chapter titles promise a Jacobite, a theft's consequences, and the Mohocks. Mrs. Wood scolds her husband for charity to Jack's mother at Willesden in one scene. Volume one ends with Saint Giles's round-house.
jack-sheppard-a-romance-vol-2-of-3:
Volume two of Ainsworth's Jack Sheppard, of 1839, carries the romance into its third epoch. Early chapters here give the Magdalene, the flash ken, and a robbery in Willesden Church. Jack breaks out of the cage at Willesden in chapter eighteen. Epoch three, the prison-breaker, is dated 1724.

Jack refuses Blueskin's plan to carry off Wood's daughter in one scene. Bess would bear no rival, he laughs. Bring Wood's wife instead, he jokes, to Blueskin's grim assent. Escapes from the New Prison and the condemned hold fill this middle volume of the romance.
jack-sheppard-a-romance-vol-3-of-3:
Volume three of Ainsworth's Jack Sheppard, of 1839, completes the prison-breaker epoch of 1724. Dollis Hill is revisited, and Jack is again captured in chapter fourteen. Blueskin undergoes the peine forte et dure, pressing, in the next chapter. Jack's portrait is painted, and the iron bar and red room follow.

Jack tears down a heap of bricks and rubbish in a cell in one escape scene. It will cost them more to build up than he took to pull down, he thinks. His mother's funeral, a return to Newgate, and Tyburn close the three volumes.
jacqueline-volume-3:
Th. Bentzon tests her heroine's pride in Jacqueline, Volume 3 of the English edition. Jacqueline at eighteen has broken with the future her family arranged. Her mother, she believes, will become Madame Marien, taking the man Jacqueline had childishly adored. Shame at her feelings drives the girl toward work.

She has passed her first Sorbonne examination with a brilliant reputation. The higher brevet, a teaching certificate, is her goal while she gives lessons in music and languages. Never marry, she vows; marriage is for rich girls bought and sold. Fortune hunter M. de Cymier sharpens her resolve by contrast. Bentzon gives the resolve sympathy and irony together. Readers in the last volume watch a girl claim a man's freedom to earn, years before French law made the claim easy.
jataka-cowell-vol-3:
The third volume of Cowell's Jataka came out in 1897, midway in the six-volume English set. H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil were among the translators from the Pali under E. B. Cowell's editorship. The tales continue in their fixed order, birth after birth.

Here the future Buddha appears in longer, richer stories, some running to small novellas of courts and quests. Tricksters test him, kings misjudge him, and his past wisdom unties each knot. The morals stay plain: generosity over grasping, calm over rage, truth over gain. Scholars mine the Jataka for early Indian life; general readers simply enjoy the tales. Volume three holds some of the best.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aargau-3:
Aargau, a canton in northern Switzerland, is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. It was formerly the only canton in which Jews were permitted to live. The townships Endingen and Lengnau, about three miles apart, formed for several centuries the Swiss ghetto. Jews there lived as protected Jews under charters renewed every sixteen years.

They could not buy land or own houses, and paid heavy taxes and poll taxes. A pillage at Lengnau in 1712 did not end the renewals, the entry reports. Federal action in July 1863 granted Swiss Jews full rights of citizens. Aargau's own council granted local citizenship in 1877.
john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume-3:
Volume three of Oliver Wendell Holmes's memoir of John Lothrop Motley reaches the historian's last work. Chapter twenty-two opens in 1874, when Motley was sixty. His final book was The Life and Death of John of Barneveld, with a view of the causes of the Thirty Years' War. Holmes calls it a history rather than a biography.

The Barneveld book forms an interlude in Motley's grand plan, the Eighty Years' Tragedy of Dutch freedom. Its last act, on the Thirty Years' War, was never written. British reviews praised the book as a worthy match for his earlier volumes. Holmes quotes the London Quarterly calling the whole series a fine, continuous story. This volume carries the memoir toward the end of Motley's laboring life.
john-marchmont-s-legacy-volume-1-of-3:
Volume one of John Marchmont's Legacy is a sensation novel by M. E. Braddon, author of Lady Audley's Secret. The third edition was published by Tinsley Brothers of London in 1863. Braddon dedicates the story to her mother. Fourteen chapters make up this first volume, from The Man with the Banner to Driven Away.

The titles name the people and the stakes: Little Mary, the Lincolnshire property, and Marchmont Towers. A young soldier returns, Olivia enters, and Mary's stepmother follows. Chapters of despair and desolation darken the middle of the volume. A figure called Paul appears before the close. This opening volume sets an inheritance tale of family pressure, love, and loss in motion.
john-marchmont-s-legacy-volume-2-of-3:
Volume two of John Marchmont's Legacy continues M. E. Braddon's sensation novel of 1863. Fourteen chapters carry the middle of the story, opening with Mary's Letter. Edward Arundel, Mrs. Marchmont, and Paul's sister move the plot forward. A stolen honeymoon and a figure risen from the grave raise the stakes.

Later chapters turn on a painting-room by the river and a paragraph in a newspaper. Edward's despair deepens, and one more sacrifice is demanded of the characters. The volume ends with a child's voice in the pavilion by the water. Braddon keeps the inheritance plot tightening, secret by secret, toward the final volume.
john-marchmont-s-legacy-volume-3-of-3:
Volume three of John Marchmont's Legacy closes M. E. Braddon's three-volume novel of 1863. It opens with Captain Arundel's Revenge, as Edward Arundel quits Lincolnshire for good. Fourteen chapters and an epilogue finish the tale. Titles promise deserted chambers, a widower's proposal, and the turning of the tide.

Belinda's wedding day and Mary's own story arrive late in the volume. The final chapter is named for the memory of wedded lives, and an epilogue follows. Edward leaves the neighborhood of Lawford Grange with a settled purpose at the start. From there Braddon resolves the legacy plot of love, money, and family claims that drove the earlier volumes.
john-marchmont-s-legacy-volumes-1-3:
John Marchmont's Legacy, in this combined edition, gathers all three volumes of M. E. Braddon's novel of 1863. Braddon, the author of Lady Audley's Secret, dedicates the story to her mother. The Tinsley Brothers third edition supplies the text. Volume one opens with The Man with the Banner and the chapter on little Mary.

The contents trace the whole arc: the Lincolnshire property, Marchmont Towers, and a young soldier's return. Olivia, Mary's stepmother, and a day of desolation follow in the first volume. Two more volumes carry the inheritance story through despair, return, and resolution. Readers get the complete sensation novel in one file, from the first banner to the epilogue.
joshua-volume-3:
Volume three of Georg Ebers's Joshua opens at chapter fifteen, beneath a sycamore tree. Miriam lies moaning while Hosea, the warrior she loves, paces in impatience. Something has suddenly towered like a mountain between them. Hosea bears promises that seem to him a merciful gift from the Most High, meant to lead his people to a fairer future.

Miriam fears he has come with terms like Uri's, a mediation her father and Moses reject. Her passion cools as she questions why he lingered and why he came without Ephraim. Ebers stages the scene under a clear, starry sky. Love and calling pull the two apart in one long, anxious night talk.
journeys-through-bookland-vol-3:
Volume three of Charles H. Sylvester's Journeys Through Bookland continues his reading plan for children, in the new edition of 1922. Lewis Carroll appears three times in the contents: The Mock Turtle's Story, Queen Alice, and The Walrus and the Carpenter. Mary Howitt's The Spider and the Fly stands beside them.

The volume also prints pieces of Robinson Crusoe and The Swiss Family Robinson. Thomas Hood's Faithless Sally Brown and William Dimond's The Mariner's Dream add verse. Aladdin and his wonderful lamp come from the Arabian Nights. A leprechaun tale by William Allingham and Beth Gelert's sad ballad widen the mix. Sylvester's set fed young readers the classics in pieces sized for them.
king-henry-vi-part-3:
An alarum opens Shakespeare's King Henry VI, Part 3, whose fuller title names the death of the Duke of York. Soldiers enter with Plantagenet's party after the sound of battle. Warwick, Edward, Richard, Norfolk, and Montague come on with him. Warwick asks at once how the King escaped their hands.

Plantagenet explains that they pursued the horsemen of the north too far. The King stole away slyly and left his men behind. Northumberland then cheered up the drooping army himself, Plantagenet says. Lord Clifford and Lord Stafford charged their main battle front abreast. The break-in puts the new fight in motion from the start.
l-abbe-constantin-volume-3:
Ludovic Halevy's novel of Longueval closes in this third volume of the English translation, which opens at chapter seven, titled Confidences. Jean Reynaud, godson of the Abbé Constantin, is now a welcome guest at the castle, where two rich young women have taken up residence. His friend Count Paul de Lavardens burns to be presented to them and teases Jean for the march he has already stolen.

Paul dreams openly of marrying Bettina and of the wealth that would come with her, while Jean hides behind his modest place as the curé's godson and the ladies' guide. The talk stays light, but money, rank, and love pull against each other in every visit. Readers who followed the sale of Longueval in the first volume here reach the story's end. The book closes on short, rueful maxims about love and quiet lives.
layamon-brut-madden-vol-3:
The third volume of Madden's 1847 edition of Layamon's Brut completes the chronicle. Layamon's verse history of Britain, written around 1200, ends with the last British king. After Arthur's fall, the poem follows the shrinking British kingdoms against the rising Saxons.

King succeeds king in brief, somber reigns until Cadwalader, the last, leaves for Rome and dies there in 689. The Britons' rule of the island ends, and the English age begins. Madden's facing translation makes the hard Middle English plain. The Brut as a whole is the first great English poem after the conquest, and its close is elegy.
lecky-england-18th-vol-3:
World war and the elder Pitt fill the third volume of Lecky's history, from 1890. The Seven Years' War spreads from Silesia to Canada and India. Britain rises toward world power on victories by land and sea across three continents.

Lecky writes at his most magisterial in these imperial chapters. He weighs strategy beside finance, and character beside chance, with calm authority. Pitt's energy drives the tale, yet the cost in debt and blood is never hidden. The volume forms a core part of his great work, showing how an island kingdom became, within one generation, the center of a worldwide empire.
lesage-gil-blas-smollett-1749-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Smollett's Gil Blas, dated 1749 in this set, completes Lesage's picaresque tale in English. Gil Blas, older now, has served many masters and seen courts and prisons from inside. The final volume brings his long education in the world to its close.

Gil rises to favor with powerful men, tastes the risks of court life, and at last withdraws to a quieter end. Lesage closed his hero's story with reflection rather than triumph, a rare note in rogue fiction. Smollett's translation, a landmark of 1749, made the whole tale part of English reading. The three volumes together chart a society through one servant's eyes.
life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-huxley-:
The third volume of Huxley's letters covers 1887 to 1895. Leonard Huxley closes his father's story with these final years. A portrait from an 1890 photograph by Downey fronts the volume. Fifteen chapters divide the correspondence of the closing period.

Readers follow Huxley through his last controversies and honors. The letters slow in pace but keep his direct, honest tone. His interest in human problems outlasted his laboratory years. Together, the three volumes form the standard life of Darwin's bulldog. McQueen printed the Downey portrait of 1890 for this volume. The final chapter carries the correspondence into 1895.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-3:
Part Three opens as the river rises in Chapter 11. Small craft become a nuisance in chute after chute. Broad-horns block cramped places and shoal water at chute heads. Profane cordialities fly between crews at every meeting.

Fog brings sudden yells, tin pans, and looming log rafts. Crews snatch engine bells and pile on steam to escape. Steamboat clerks, Twain claims, carried assortments of religious tracts. Twenty times daily they cramped around bars behind drifting small-fry. Clerks carried the tracts twenty times a day, he insists. Broad-horns waited in the worst locality, the chute's head.
littre-dictionary-1863-vol-3:
Volume 3 of Littré's Dictionary carried the work through the heart of the alphabet. The dictionary had been appearing since 1863, and Littré, aging and often ill, drove it forward without lowering his standard. His method never changed: history first, with evidence for every sense.

The middle volumes hold some of the richest words in French. Littré gives each its genealogy, its old spellings, and its shifts of meaning across the centuries. Quotations from poets, chroniclers, and scientists crowd the pages. The great work's middle march shows no flagging, course by course of the crown of French lexicography. Scholars still cite Littré where later dictionaries are silent, above all for older French. Volume 3 is the project at its fullest stretch, the language's biography at its widest point.
lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-3:
Volume 3 carries George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta into Book 3. It opens at a dinner at Mrs. Lawrence's house, where a Horse Guards orderly brings a large parcel. Lord Ormont keeps the company waiting while Aminta strains to know what has come.

The chapters move from Cuper's schoolboys to a 'war' at Olmer, the family estate. Old lovers become new friends, and a secret is fished out without angling. Two roads lead toward Steignton as feelings shift and alliances change. Meredith mixes comedy with real feeling in these scenes. The volume tightens the knot between Ormont, Aminta, and Weyburn.
lucian-works-fowler-vol-3:
The Fowler brothers' third volume of Lucian continues their complete English translation of 1905. Lucian's output was huge, and this volume keeps the laughter coming. Imaginary voyages and mock trials of the dead appear among its pieces.

Lucian's jokes preserve a vivid picture of educated belief in the Roman Empire. He parodies historians, tragedians, and religious enthusiasts with a reporter's eye. One famous piece sails to the moon long before science fiction existed. The Fowlers render his Greek into clear, lively Edwardian prose. Satire here doubles as social history of the second century. Few ancient authors entertain while informing this reliably across so many subjects.
lyell-principles-of-geology-vol-3:
Charles Lyell closed his Principles of Geology with a third volume in the early 1830s. After setting out his method, he applied it to the rocks themselves in detail. Water-laid and fire-made causes take center stage in these chapters.

Lyell sorts strata, fossils, and landforms to show gradual change at work. His system made a very old earth, and even ancient human history, seem plausible. Few science books have shifted so many minds at once. The volume completes the founding work of modern geology. Generations of geology students learned the science largely through Lyell's framing of it.
lyra-graeca-edmonds-loeb-vol-3:
Stesichorus, Ibycus, Simonides, and Bacchylides headline the third Loeb volume of Lyra Graeca, in J. M. Edmonds's edition and English version. These poets of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE wrote for cities, kings, and victors across the Greek world. Little of them survives whole, and much came back only from papyrus finds.

Simonides made the epitaph an art and was famed for his memory and his tears for the dead. Bacchylides, his nephew, sang victory odes that rival those of Pindar. Edmonds sets out the fragments with notes on each torn line. The volume completes his gathering of the lyric remains that founded Western song.
madame-chrysantheme-volume-3:
Volume 3 of Madame Chrysanthème was Gutenberg etext number 80. It carries on Pierre Loti's diary of a summer in Japan. The French Academy crowned Loti among its Immortals for such work. His hero is himself, a naval officer far from home.

By this part the Nagasaki season is well advanced. Chrysanthème and her officer husband live their arranged, fragile union. Loti fills pages with processions, music, and harbor scenes. Under the charm runs a note of coming parting. Ships and orders govern a sailor's heart, and his stay must end. The volume lets the reader feel time closing on the summer.
made-to-measure-deep-waters-part-3:
Made to Measure is a comic tale by W. W. Jacobs, from his Deep Waters. This is part three of that collection of short stories. Mr. Mott fetches his niece from the station with great pride. Her photograph had made him nervous about claiming the right girl.

Miss Garland steps down pretty and well dressed, tired of London. She calls his little old town beautiful and peaceful. The lonely old man hopes she will stay a long time. She hints at other things than noise that upset her in town. Jacobs builds his quiet comedy from such small hints. His tales of clerks and watermen are models of dry humor.
mahavastu-senart-vol-3:
The third and last volume of Senart's Mahavastu came out in 1897 and completes his great edition. Le Mahavastu closes here with the last runs of the Buddha legend in Sanskrit. The full work had taken Senart fifteen long years of labor to print.

The closing books bring the long chain of past lives toward the final birth and waking. Kings, gods, and common folk cross the Buddha's path in tale after tale. Senart's finished edition set the standard text for this great Buddhist scripture. Students of early Buddhism still work from his three volumes today.
master-tales-of-mystery-volume-3:
Francis J. Reynolds gathered Master Tales of Mystery, Volume 3. Six tales by Arthur B. Reeve lead the book. They star Craig Kennedy, the famed sleuth of that day.

Reeve's tales name a poisoned pen, a silent bullet, and a steel door. Paul L. Ford adds a great train robbery tale. Max Pemberton, George B. McCutcheon, and Burton E. Stevenson add more. The set mixes crime, fear, and clever proof for fans of short thrills. Joseph Ernest and Marjorie Pickthall close the contents page. Short, sharp cases suit readers who like a puzzle solved in one sitting.
matthew-paris-english-history-giles-vol-:
J. A. Giles's third volume of Matthew Paris runs from 1259 to 1273 and closes the set with the general index to Matthew and to Roger of Wendover. The chronicle that Matthew built at Saint Albans here covers the Barons' War in full. It is the last stretch of the fullest English history of the thirteenth century.

The barons under Simon de Montfort beat the king at Lewes and rule for a year, then fall at Evesham in 1265. Prince Edward rebuilds royal power, and the young Henry's reign ends in 1272. Matthew had died in 1259, and his brothers of Saint Albans carried the tale on. The index opens the whole vast chronicle to the reader.
memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-delusio:
Volume three of Mackay's Popular Delusions treats learned folly at length. Book one covers the alchemists and their long search. They sought the philosopher's stone and the water of life.

Geber, Avicenna, Albertus Magnus, and Roger Bacon stand in part one. Part two runs through Paracelsus, Dr. Dee, and the Rosicrucians. Count de St. Germain and Cagliostro close that long line of adepts. Book two treats fortune telling, and book three treats the magnetisers. A head on philosophical delusions stands after the magnetisers. Learned men, Mackay shows, can chase folly as hard as crowds.
memoirs-of-henry-hunt-esq-volume-3:
Volume three of Henry Hunt's memoirs opens with a scene of violence. A young woman lay senseless, struck down near a procession. Her scalp wound ran four inches long, the text states.

Blood streamed down her white gown as she came to her senses. Her cap and clothes were torn to rags in the attack. She ran to Hunt and told her wrongs before the crowd. Four to five thousand Bristolians stood by, horror struck at the sight. Hunt says he knows the villain who struck the blow. Outrage drives this volume's start more than self praise.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Book three of Madame de Montespan's memoirs opens at chapter thirty five. M. de Lauzun and Mademoiselle de Montpensier head that chapter. The King settles a match, and a secret union follows in the heads.

Mademoiselle falls hard for Lauzun, a man she takes for a lover. She drops her proud reserve and hides her love in glances and signs. At last she hands him a written offer of marriage in a recess. Lauzun feigns awe, sheds tears, and feeds her passion with wiles. The King sends Lauzun to Pignerol in the heads that follow. Gifts from the princess mark her vain hope to free him.
memoirs-of-marguerite-de-valois-queen-of:
Book three of this set holds a History of the House of Valois. The sample names no author for that history in its heads. It starts with Charles, Comte de Valois, brother of Philip the Fair.

When Charles IV's queen bears a daughter, the barons must choose an heir. The peers hold that the crown can pass to no woman, Froissart says. Philip of Valois takes the throne and founds a new royal house. He proves a stern master who strikes the great lords when he can. Edward III's claim, through his mother, is weighed and set aside. Lawyers, the text says, backed the new king against the lords.
merivale-romans-empire-vol-3:
Good emperors rule in the third volume of Merivale's History of the Romans, issued in eighteen sixty-five. Vespasian restores order, and the line runs through Trajan to Marcus Aurelius. Rome enjoys its long golden age of wide peace and wise government under the Flavians and Antonines.

Merivale shows power joined to wisdom across a favored century. Roads, laws, and cities flourish from Britain to Syria in his account. He clearly loves good government and says why it matters. The volume forms the bright center of his work. The Empire stands at its height, ruled for once by wise men.
michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-swords-vol:
Volume Three closes Gilbert Parker's romance of Michel and Angele amid Elizabethan court intrigue. Its sample chapter studies the Earl of Leicester, the Queen's longtime favorite. Parker describes how Leicester rose by subterranean means, checkmating Spanish, German, and French diplomacy. Yet the same passage condemns the small, scheming habits that built his power.

Parker argues that practiced intriguers lose all sense of proportion. They must scheme even when the stakes are trifling. Against such a court, the Huguenot lovers' fate is decided. The closing volume gives the romance its darkest portrait of power at Elizabeth's court.
milman-history-jews-vol-3:
Maccabees to catastrophe fill the third volume of Milman's History of the Jews, from 1829. The people endure Greek kings, win brief freedom under the Maccabees, then pass under Rome's hard hand. Jerusalem falls in the year 70, the Temple burns, and the dispersion of the Jews begins.

Milman closes his pioneering work with that vast sorrow. He writes the tragedy with restraint, learning, and evident feeling throughout. A clergyman's fairness toward another faith marked the whole enterprise. The three volumes together founded modern Jewish historiography in English, and they still reward readers who want the story told as history, not legend.
mirk-abbey-volume-2-of-3:
James Payn published Mirk Abbey with Hurst and Blackett in London in 1866. This is the second of its three volumes. The volume opens with Lady Lisgard calling her attendant Mary, Mistress Forest, for a serious talk. Mary's respectful tone hides a resolve the narrator marks at once: she has decided to answer no.

Chapter titles promise a confession, a breach of post-office rules, and an uncheerful picnic. The action moves to Epsom and turns on a letter from Paris. Characters named Withers and Arthur Haldane maneuver through thrust and counter-thrust. Payn builds a mid-Victorian tale of secrets, letters, and household power.
mirk-abbey-volume-3-of-3:
The third volume of James Payn's Mirk Abbey, published in London in 1866, closes the three-volume novel. Its chapters introduce Madame de Castellan and a memorial window at the abbey. Titles like Fled, The Uninvited Guest, and Out of the Cage quicken the pace. The volume ends with The Reconciliation, Ralph's Appeal, and Dying Words.

Payn resolves the secrets that Lady Lisgard's household has carried through the earlier volumes. Jacob's guard-ship and a triumphal arch widen the scene beyond the abbey. Three-volume novels like this one supplied the circulating libraries of Victorian England. This final volume delivers the confrontations and settlements its readers awaited.
miscellaneous-writings-and-speeches-volu:
Volume Three of Macaulay's miscellaneous writings turns to his Encyclopaedia Britannica contributions. Five biographical articles anchor the volume. They treat Francis Atterbury, John Bunyan, Oliver Goldsmith, Samuel Johnson, and William Pitt. The dates run from 1853 to 1859, the last years of Macaulay's life.

The volume also gathers his miscellaneous poems and inscriptions. Early pieces include an epitaph on Henry Martyn and lines to Pitt's memory. A Radical War Song and two battle ballads follow, on Moncontour and Naseby. The Naseby poem is credited to a mock Puritan serjeant with an enormous hyphenated name, Macaulay's joke in full view.
mohawks-a-novel-volume-1-of-3:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon's Mohawks appeared in London in 1886, in three volumes. The title page credits only the author of Lady Audley's Secret, Vixen, and Ishmael. John and Robert Maxwell published the novel from Fleet Street. This first volume's chapters carry poetic mottoes as their titles.

The opening chapter is called One That Doth Wear Himself Away in Loneness. The second is A Tedious Road the Weary Wretch Returns. Such headings promise a sensation plot of suffering and endurance.
